entry.title: Slack Business+ Slackbot limit: 15 messages per user a week (Nov 11, 2026)
entry.summary:
Slack's pricing page changed overnight in two ways that matter for anyone paying for its AI features.
## Change 1: Slackbot gets a weekly cap on Business+
On Nov 10, the Business+ plan described Slackbot as "Your personal AI agent that understands conversations, files, and projects in Slack. Plan limits apply." On Nov 11 the same row reads: "Find answers, summarize channels, and work across your apps. 15 messages per user each week. Contact sales to add more." Business+ is listed at $15 per user a month billed annually, or $18 billed monthly. The feature is also renamed from "Slackbot (personal AI agent)" to plain "Slackbot" across the plan table, and the comparison table adds "Consumption based" and "Usage limits" rows.
## Change 2: Enterprise+ gets a price, and unlimited Slackbot
Enterprise+ used to say "Contact sales for pricing." It now shows "$45 USD per user / month, when paying annually," still with a Contact Sales button. Its Slackbot row now reads "Unlimited Slackbot" with "It’s unlimited for your whole team."
What stays the same: The note that Business+ customers on Salesforce invoice plans can unlock higher message limits by buying Flex Credits through Salesforce is unchanged apart from formatting. Pro still lists Slackbot without a stated number.
What you can do: Business+ admins should check how heavily their teams use Slackbot; 15 messages a week is about three a workday.

entry.title: Dave & Buster's privacy policy (Nov 4, 2026): sells data to data brokers, CCTV video, keystroke tracking
entry.summary:
Dave & Buster's posted a new privacy policy marked "Effective Date: November 4, 2026". It replaces a notice marked "Effective Date: January 1, 2020", which was still live when the Wayback Machine captured the page on October 15, 2026. We compared that capture with the live page on November 11, 2026. This is a full rewrite, not a few edits. It now covers the website, the app, and anyone who will "play games or enjoy other digital experiences at our locations", which means the arcade floor as well as the website.
## Change 1: from "We do not sell" to naming data brokers
The 2020 notice's sharing section began: "We do not sell or otherwise share personal information about you, except as described in this Privacy Notice." Its California section did say that ad partners' access "may be considered a sale under CCPA under certain circumstances" and that D&B "engages in online advertising practices that may potentially be considered 'sales' under the CCPA." The new policy states it outright: "We sell or share this information with advertising networks, data brokers and other companies involved in digital advertising to assist us in delivering personalized ads to you." The data in question is "personal identifiers (including email address; phone number; and unique identifier) and internet or other electronic activity information." The policy says this happens "by allowing third parties to place cookies or other tracking technologies on our website" and "by sharing information with our advertising partners." It lists "Advertising companies and data brokers" as the third parties that receive personal information, and "advertising companies and data brokers" among the places D&B gets information from. (The 2020 notice already listed "Third-party data resellers" as a source.)
## Change 2: tools that capture keystrokes
A new cookies section says D&B lets third parties use tracking tools "so that they can provide analytics information and deliver targeted ads tailored to you", and that "This may include tools that capture your keystrokes, mouse clicks, screen touches, and information about when, how and from where you accessed our Sites." It names one tool: "Among other tools, we use Google Ads." The 2020 notice didn't mention keystrokes. It only said data "might be collected by us or 3rd parties, such as Smartlook.com, s.r.o.", without saying what that company collects.
## Change 3: CCTV video, IDs and in-store data
The list of what D&B collects now includes "Video of you captured on CCTV security cameras installed in our locations", "drivers' license or other identification card information", "status as a first responder", "Power Card and Rewards accounts information and balances", and "information collected electronically from you in our stores." The 2020 notice mentioned Power Card purchases but none of the others. The policy says it has "collected these same categories of personal information in the 12 months before the date of this Policy", so this describes what D&B was already doing, not only what it plans to do. It also lists "Inferences drawn from personal information", and says D&B has disclosed "video of you captured on CCTV security cameras" for business purposes in the past 12 months, without saying to whom.
## What D&B says your data is worth
The policy adds a "Notice of Financial Incentive" for the Dave & Buster's Rewards program. It says D&B collects "your name and phone number and track your associated purchases so we can send you personalized offers". Then it puts a price on it: "We estimate the value of personal information as less than a dollar, based upon the value of bonus Game Chips."
## What got better
Some of the changes help you. Opt-outs must be honored "no later than 15 business days after receipt of your request", down from "no later than 45 days" in the 2020 notice. D&B now says "We recognize the Global Privacy Control signal when sent from IP addresses in states with privacy laws that apply to us", although only "for that browser only". It says that "if we know you are under the age of 18, we won't knowingly sell or share your personal information for targeted advertising". The 2020 notice only promised not to knowingly sell the data of children under 13. The policy now lists rights for residents of 17 states, and says rights for Alabama, Louisiana and Oklahoma residents come when those laws take effect in 2027.
## Odd details
The SMS section ends: "You can also reach us at privacy@mainevent.com." Main Event is the family-entertainment chain Dave & Buster's has owned since 2022 (Wikipedia). Main Event's own privacy policy, "Effective January 1, 2026", doesn't contain the data-broker, CCTV or keystroke language. D&B also says "We do not respond to the DNT or 'Do Not Track' signal."
## Why this matters now
In October 2025, two California residents filed a proposed class action in federal court in the Northern District of California. They allege that daveandbusters.com kept sending browsing data to Meta, Google, TikTok, Microsoft and X after visitors clicked "Reject All" on the cookie banner (National Law Review, October 30, 2025). These are allegations, not findings. The new policy describes in much more detail the tracking that suit is about.
Coverage (checked Nov 11, 2026): we found no news coverage of the November 4 policy. Search results show only the policy itself.

entry.title: Chase Digital Services Agreement (Oct 2026): External AI login bar, Trusted Device from Jan 1, 2027
entry.summary:
Chase's Digital Services Agreement, the contract for Chase Online, Chase Mobile, Chase Business Online, Chase Point of Sale, J.P. Morgan Online and J.P. Morgan Mobile, was last updated October 2026. We fetched the current PDF at static.chasecdn.com (dsa1_la.pdf) on November 11, 2026. A longer related PDF at the same library (dsa_la.pdf) is last updated November 2026 and opens with the same two dated changes, plus new Zelle Brokerage terms; the quotes below are from dsa1_la.pdf unless noted.
The October 2026 PDF opens with a "We're making key changes" cover. Two dates matter.
## Change 1: External AI, automated tools and data aggregators may not use your login (effective October 27, 2026)
The cover says: "Effective October 27, 2026, we have made changes to ratify your obligation to not share credentials with third parties and that third parties — including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators — are prohibited from using your Login Credentials to access the Digital Platforms or your accounts or Services thereon. We permit third-party applications and tools, including External AI, to access customer account data through approved application programming interfaces ("APIs") with your authorization."
The same paragraph continues: "If you have shared your Login Credentials with any third party, you must change those credentials to ensure that the third party can no longer use them or access your information through the Digital Platforms."
That wording is repeated in the body under "Sharing Your Login Credentials with Third Parties is Prohibited." The definitions section says "External AI: means, collectively, Third-party AI and Third-party AI Agent, and includes any provider thereof." A "Third-party AI Agent" includes "any AI-based software or service provided by a third party that takes autonomous, semi-autonomous, or non-autonomous action on behalf of, or at the instruction of, any person (human or entity), including you." "Login Credentials" are "PINs, user IDs, passwords, biometrics, security keys, syncable authenticators (e.g., passkeys), or any other means of accessing the Digital Platforms or your accounts or Services thereon."
If you still let a third party, "including External AI," access the platforms or your accounts, a long "Consequences" list says you "expressly authorize that third party to transact in your account," that Chase will "rely on, and treat as evidence of your authorization, any actions taken or instructions given by the third party as if you personally took or gave those actions or instructions," and that you "assume all risks and losses associated with such access or use." Chase also "reserve[s] the right to deny, decline, suspend, or terminate your access to the Digital Platforms, your accounts, or Services — including access facilitated by External AI or other third party — or to close your account(s), at any time, in our sole discretion and without notice. This may render External AI or your account(s) non-functional."
What it replaces (Wayback, fetched November 11, 2026): the Internet Archive has two captures of this same dsa1_la.pdf URL, from December 30, 2020 and February 19, 2022. We fetched the February 19, 2022 file. It is last updated 4/1/2021. Its "Passwords & Other Sensitive Information" section says you agree "to protect and keep confidential your Card number, account number, PIN, user ID, Password, or other means of accessing your accounts via the Digital Platforms." It also says: "If you permit any other person or entity, including any data aggregation service providers, to use the Digital Platforms or to access or use your Card numbers, account numbers, PINs, user IDs, Passwords, or other means to access your accounts, you are responsible for any transactions and activities performed from your accounts and for any use of your personal and account information by any person or entity to whom they may provide that personal and account information." There is no "External AI" definition, no ban on automated tools using your login, no instruction to change a password you have already shared, and no Trusted Device section. We could not retrieve a later pre-October 2026 capture of the related dsa_la.pdf from the Wayback Machine in this session (the archive listed captures through September 26, 2026, but returned HTTP 429). Intermediate versions may exist; the comparison above is to the 2022 capture of this same filename.
## Change 2: From January 1, 2027, Chase may require the mobile app and a Trusted Device, and may deny access until you comply
The cover says: "Effective January 1, 2027, we may require you to (i) download and use our mobile application, and (ii) use a Trusted Device, as defined in this agreement to verify your identity. Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law."
The body section "Authentication via Trusted Device" repeats the may-require and may-deny language but does not repeat the January 1, 2027 date: "To help protect your account from fraud and unauthorized access, we may require you to download and use our mobile application, and use a Trusted Device, as defined in this Agreement, to verify your identity. Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law. You should use only your personal device – one you control and only you use – as your Trusted Device. If you lose access to your Trusted Device (for example, if it is lost or stolen), you may need to verify a new one via Trusted Device Enrollment, as defined in this Agreement, which could temporarily delay your ability to access our Digital Platforms, accounts, or complete transactions and other banking activities."
A Trusted Device is defined as "A smartphone that (1) runs a Supported Mobile Operating System, and (2) we recognize as your trusted device after you use our mobile applications (for example, the Chase Mobile® app) and meet our security requirements, which we may modify from time to time in our sole discretion." Trusted Device Enrollment "may include specific identity verification and authentication methods (for example, taking a photo of an acceptable form of identification with your smartphone camera)."
Chase's customer FAQ (chase.com/personal/banking/education/basics/trusteddevice, fetched November 11, 2026) matches that definition: "A trusted device is a smartphone that you’ve verified with the Chase Mobile app in accordance with requirements established by Chase." It also says: "Currently, only smartphones with the Chase Mobile app installed and a supported operating system (such as iOS 16.0 or later or Android 11 or later) can be trusted devices. Tablets, laptops, desktop computers, and iPads are not eligible at this time." And: "For your security, only use your own device to access your Chase account, and don't enroll a device you share." The FAQ does not mention the January 1, 2027 date.
What you can do: if you have given your Chase password to an app, an aggregator or an AI assistant, change it. Before January 1, 2027, if you want to keep using Chase in a browser, be ready to enroll a personal smartphone in the Chase Mobile app; the agreement says Chase may deny access until you do, unless the law requires an accommodation. If you only have a tablet, laptop or shared phone, the FAQ says those are not eligible as Trusted Devices.
Coverage (checked November 11, 2026): a November 4 Hunton Andrews Kurth alert in the National Law Review, "Major banks move to block or limit customer-directed AI agents," discusses Chase alongside Schwab, Citi and Wells Fargo. Its table dates Chase's action to an October 13, 2026 earnings-call remark by Jamie Dimon and describes "an updated Digital Services Agreement (effective Jan. 1, 2027)" as providing that a customer who gives an AI agent access "authorizes everything that AI agent does." The October 2026 PDF we fetched dates the External AI and credential-sharing rules to October 27, 2026, and uses January 1, 2027 for the Trusted Device and mobile-app requirement. The "authorizes everything" consequences are in the current PDF body, not only as a January 1 term. We did not find a consumer news story that quotes the October 27 External AI bar or the "you must change those credentials" line.

entry.title: Microsoft privacy statement update: workplace data sources, logged-out age checks (Nov 2026)
entry.summary:
Microsoft revised its privacy statement. We compared the Nov 10 capture with Nov 9.
## Change 1: A new source of personal data
The list of sources Microsoft collects data from (which already included "Publicly available sources, such as open public sector, academic, and commercial data sets") gains a new line: "Companies that provide workplace and productivity data for research, development, and improvement of our products and services." The statement doesn't name those companies.
## Change 2: Age protections without signing in
The age-appropriate experiences section, which already covered age range signals from app stores and sharing age group information with third-party apps, adds: "In services you can use without logging in, we may use device-based information to help us apply age-appropriate protections."
## Change 3: More device data named
Device data examples now read: "IP addresses, age of the device, device identifiers and type, device language and locale settings, nearby networks," adding device age, type and language settings.
## Change 4: Personalized offers off still uses some data
A new paragraph says that if you turn off Personalized offers in Windows, Microsoft "may use basic account data and contextual info about your device" to avoid irrelevant tips and ads, for example "your active subscriptions to avoid showing you ads for products you have already purchased."
## Change 5: Phone Link rewritten, location sharing added
The separate Android and iPhone sections of Phone Link were merged into one "linked mobile experiences" section that also covers apps such as WhatsApp. It adds a Location sharing feature: "You can access location information from your mobile device after you choose to enable this feature." Microsoft still says it does not store the content of your texts, call history, photos, files or notifications on its servers, except where a feature says otherwise.
The page does not state a new effective date in our capture.

entry.title: Dropbox terms change Jan 1, 2027: free accounts closed after 6 months inactive, 18+ only
entry.summary:
Dropbox posted new Terms of Service and a new Privacy Policy on September 1, 2026. Both take effect January 1, 2027. We compared the new terms (dropbox.com/terms2026, marked "Posted: September 1, 2026" and "Effective: January 1, 2027") with the terms in force today ("Posted: January 7, 2025"), and did the same for the privacy policy (in force since May 30, 2025). We fetched all four on Nov 10, 2026. Dropbox's announcement leads with a new feature, using one account for several personal and team workspaces. Several changes for free users are listed further down.
## Change 1: Free accounts can be closed after 6 months, not 12
The current terms let Dropbox suspend or terminate your access with notice if you "don't have a Paid Account and haven't accessed our Services for 12 consecutive months." The new terms say "6 consecutive months." The rest of the clause stays the same: Dropbox says it will give "reasonable advance notice via the email address associated with your account" and a chance to "export Your Stuff" first. Dropbox's announcement adds: "We'll continue to provide notice before doing so."
This matters most to people on Dropbox Basic, the free 2 GB plan, who keep old files there and rarely sign in. Dropbox's help page on inactive accounts (checked Nov 10, 2026) still describes the old rule. It says activity means "log-ins and file activity (adding, editing, or deleting) anywhere on Dropbox during the past 12 months," and that "Logging in again will reset the 12-month clock." The page also says: "If we don't notify you that your account is inactive, your account won't be deleted due to inactivity," and that you'll get "multiple reminder emails" with the scheduled deletion date. Activity on Dropbox Sign or DocSend "doesn't count."
When the clock matters: if the six-month test applies as soon as the terms take effect, a free account nobody has signed in to since before July 1, 2026 would already be past six months on January 1, 2027. Dropbox hasn't said whether it counts inactivity from before January 1.
## Change 2: You must be 18 to use Dropbox
The current terms say you must be "at least 13 if you reside in the United States, and 16 if you reside anywhere else." The new terms say "you must be at least 18," and add: "Dropbox may use and rely on information from third parties, including age signals from app stores, for the purpose of enforcing this restriction." Dropbox's help page says: "Starting January 1, 2027, you must be at least 18 years old in order to use Dropbox." Neither the terms nor the help pages say what happens to accounts that 13- to 17-year-olds already have, or to their files.
## Change 3: To say no, you now have to delete your account
The current terms say that if you don't agree to an update, "please cancel your account and stop using the Services," and that "continuing to use or access the Services" means you agree. The new terms say "please cancel and delete your account," and "By maintaining an account after the updates come into effect, you agree to be bound by the revised Terms." Dropbox's help page spells it out: "You will agree to our updated Terms by maintaining a Dropbox account after the effective date of the updated Terms." So an account you never open still counts as agreeing on January 1.
## Other changes
Refunds: "Refunds are only issued if required by law" becomes "Refunds are only issued in limited circumstances or if required by law." Dropbox's help page calls this a clarification that "we may also grant refunds in other limited circumstances." The terms don't say what those circumstances are.
Price-change notice: the promise of "no less than 30 days' advance notice" of a new renewal price now starts with "Unless a shorter notice period is necessitated by applicable law." You still get the chance to cancel before the new fee.
Several accounts on one email: the new terms treat each team or personal workspace you join as "its own account" and say "Actions taken on one account, including suspension, deletion, termination, or removal from a Dropbox Team, may impact your access to or use of the Services." If an admin removes you from a team and deletes that account, "you may be unable to access your other accounts until you change the email address for those accounts." And: "If you have multiple accounts associated with the same email address, and we suspend or terminate your access to the Services, that action may apply to all associated accounts."
Work email addresses: today, your organization "may be able to block" a personal Dropbox account opened with a work address. The new terms add that "even if your organization does not block your use of Dropbox, we may block your use of Dropbox" until you move to a Dropbox Team or switch to a personal email address.
Privacy policy: the new policy adds that team admins "may be able to view changes in account state for your other accounts, such as suspension, deletion, termination, account capture, or removal from another Dropbox Team," and a way to appeal privacy decisions (email privacy@dropbox.com). It also now points straight to its FAQ "for more detail regarding how Your Stuff may be used to improve the Services." That FAQ says (the sentence has been there since at least April 2025, per the Wayback Machine): "We may build models that identify keywords and topics from a given document. These models may be trained on your documents and metadata, and power features within Dropbox such as improved search relevance, auto-sorting and organization features, and document summaries."
## How 6 months compares
Google says it may delete a personal Google Account "if you are inactive across Google for at least two years" (Google Account Help, checked Nov 10, 2026). Microsoft's Services Agreement (effective Sept 30, 2026) says you "must sign into your Outlook.com inbox and your OneDrive (separately) at least once in a one-year period, otherwise we will close your Outlook.com inbox and your OneDrive for you," and sign in to the Microsoft account itself at least once every two years. From January 1, Dropbox's limit for free accounts is half of OneDrive's and a quarter of Google's. Among other cloud storage services (terms checked Nov 10, 2026): Apple's iCloud terms say Apple may terminate an account "upon 30 days’ prior notice via email" if it "has been inactive for one (1) year"; pCloud says "Free pCloud accounts that have been inactive for 12 months, will be permanently deleted, along with the files inside"; MEGA is stricter than Dropbox, listing as a reason to suspend or terminate that "you are using a free account and that account has been inactive for over 3 months and you have been given notice to act."
In order, from longest to shortest: Google 2 years; Microsoft (Outlook.com and OneDrive) 1 year; Apple iCloud 1 year; pCloud 12 months; Dropbox 12 months today, 6 months from January 1, 2027; MEGA over 3 months, after notice. Proton went the other way this month: it now waits 24 months, not 12, before it can delete an unused free account (see our Nov 6 report on Proton).
What you can do: If you have a free Dropbox account you care about, sign in at dropbox.com or in the app before January 1 and at least every few months after that. Dropbox counts log-ins and adding, editing or deleting files. Watch for Dropbox emails about inactivity, including at old email addresses: the help page notes that many people have more than one account. If you'd rather not accept the new terms, the only way out is to download your files and delete your account before January 1, 2027. Under-18s, and parents of teens with accounts, should download any files they want to keep now.
Coverage (checked Nov 10, 2026): Dropbox announced the update on its blog on Sept 1, 2026, and in its help center. SMBtech (Sept 20) covered the 18+ age limit and the six-month window; Security Online, WebProNews and the UK site TrustList covered the six-month window; and the independent Dropbox Watchdog site published a clause-by-clause comparison that also noted the inactive-account help page still says 12 months. We found no coverage in major consumer or tech outlets (rechecked Nov 10, 2026), and none that compared the new limit with Google, Microsoft, Apple iCloud, pCloud and MEGA.

entry.title: Netlify Dec 4 terms: verified domains can see staff accounts and may absorb them
entry.summary:
Netlify published a changelog on Nov 4, 2026 saying it updated its Self-Serve Subscription Agreement, Privacy Statement and Acceptable Use Policy, and that the changes take effect on December 4, 2026. We compared the live Self-Serve Subscription Agreement PDF (Last Updated: November 4, 2026) to the prior PDF archived by the Wayback Machine on Oct 16, 2026 (Last Updated: October 1, 2025), and read the live Privacy Statement (Last updated: November 4, 2026).
## Change 1: Verified Domains can see that your account exists
Section 6.6 is new. It is not in the October 1, 2025 agreement. The November 4 text says that if Netlify verifies that an organization owns or controls the domain of the email address on your account, Netlify may disclose to that organization "the existence of Customer's account, its plan type, and information about the sites under that account that are publicly accessible on the Services, such as their site names, URLs, and when they were last deployed."
The same section says Netlify will not, under 6.6, disclose payment information, or your name, email or username "other than as they may appear in any account names, site names, or URLs," and will not disclose Customer Content that is not publicly accessible. "Verification alone does not give that organization access to or control over Customer's account."
Netlify's own changelog puts the same point in plain English: an organization that proves the domain "may show it that your account exists, its plan type, and the names, URLs, and last deploy dates of your publicly accessible sites," and never shows your name, email, username or payment information that way.
## Change 2: Account moves are restated, with Customer Content named
The October 1, 2025 agreement already warned, in the preamble before section 1: if the domain of your account email is owned or controlled by an entity that has (or later gets) a direct subscription agreement with Netlify, "your account may be rolled into and consolidated with that organization's account after notification to you," and if you do not change the email, "your account will be controlled by the entity."
The November 4 agreement moves that rule into section 2.1 (Accounts and Email Addresses). It says the account "may be consolidated into that organization's account after notice to Customer." If you do not change the email "within the period stated in such notice, the account, including its Customer Content, will be controlled by that organization."
So Dec 4 is not the first day Netlify could absorb a domain-matched account. What is new for readers is the pairing with Verified Domains visibility, the notice-window wording, and the explicit line that Customer Content goes with the moved account.
## Change 3: Privacy Statement adds Verified Organizations and an opt-out
The Privacy Statement dated November 4, 2026 adds an "Organization domains" processing purpose that points to sections 6.6 and 2.1, and a "Verified Organizations" disclosure category with the same account-exists / plan / public-site fields. Section 8 says you can "Opt out of domain visibility at any time by contacting us at privacy@netlify.com," and that changing your account email to one outside the organization's domain before the date in a move notice stops the transfer. The changelog repeats both steps.
## What stays the same
Enterprise Master Subscription Agreement customers are still under that agreement, not this self-serve one. The November 4 agreement also keeps Netlify's line that it will not use Customer Content to train or fine-tune AI models unless the customer opts in.
## What you can do
Personal projects on a work email are the risk case. Change the email, or email privacy@netlify.com for visibility opt-out, and watch for any move notice after Dec 4.
Coverage (checked Nov 9, 2026): Netlify's own changelog is the announcement. The independent tracker toolongdidnotread.it flagged the Privacy Statement change. entry.title: Vrew Dec 1, 2026: one account per person and AI analysis of project content
entry.summary:
Vrew published a help article announcing updates to its Terms of Service and Privacy Policy effective December 1, 2026. The quotes below are from that notice's own current/revised comparison tables and retention table (fetched Nov 9, 2026). We are treating the vendor notice as the primary source for this due-soon item; we did not re-fetch every linked revised PDF beyond the notice.
## Change 1: One account per person, not per email
Vrew's notice says that starting December 1, "you may use only one account, even if you have different email addresses." Its table moves the rule from "The Service supports only one account per email address" (Article 5, Paragraph 1) to "Only one account is permitted per User for the Service" (Article 6, Paragraph 1).
It also says multiple people may not share one account, "including within companies and teams," and asks users to prepare separate accounts before December 1. Separately, Vrew says it is working on a company/team way to manage multiple accounts and will share details later.
## Change 2: AI analysis of project content and editing history
The Privacy Policy table replaces a footnote that said the company does not use project files for training and does not arbitrarily access or analyze project content without consent. The revised footnote says the company "analyzes the contents and assets of projects and the user's editing history using artificial intelligence" to provide a personalized editing experience, and "does not use the user's information for training artificial intelligence other than for this purpose."
A new processing row lists "Project categories, summaries, and assets; your editing history" for "Provision of personalized services," retained "Until you delete your account." The notice says analysis covers images, videos, audio and captions (assets), turned into topic categories and content summaries.
## What you can do
Object through in-app chat support by December 1, or delete the account. Vrew says that if you do not object by the effective date, it will treat that as agreement.
Coverage (checked Nov 9, 2026): We found no press coverage of the December 1 Vrew Terms/Privacy update beyond Vrew's own help article.

entry.title: Rakuten cash back rates are now personalized and can differ by member (Oct 23, 2026 terms)
entry.summary:
Rakuten (the cash back site formerly called Ebates) updated both its Terms & Conditions and its Privacy Policy on October 23, 2026. We compared the live terms (fetched Nov 9, 2026) with the previous version, dated October 15, 2025, as archived by the Wayback Machine on April 15, 2026. We compared the live privacy policy with the version dated December 18, 2025, archived July 12, 2026. Rakuten says it has more than 17 million members.
## Change 1: Your cash back rate is now "personalized"
The old terms described cash back as a cut of Rakuten's referral fee: "Rakuten gives a portion of this fee to its Members as Cash Back." They said cash back amounts "VARY BY AFFILIATE STORE AND PRODUCT CATEGORY."
The October 23 terms add a new sentence to Section 4: "Rewards rates and offers available through the Services are personalized and may vary by Member based on factors including your account history, shopping behavior, and membership status as described in our Privacy Policy. As a result, the Rewards rate available to you may differ from the rate available to other Members for the same Brand or product."
The exclusions section changes in the same way. "CASH BACK AMOUNTS VARY BY AFFILIATE STORE AND PRODUCT CATEGORY" becomes "REWARD AMOUNTS VARY BY BRAND, PRODUCT CATEGORY, BY MEMBER, AND BY SURFACE." The terms don't define "surface." Read plainly, it means the rate can also depend on where you see the offer (website, app, browser extension, or another channel).
The privacy policy now says it too. To its section on personalizing the service, Rakuten added: "The offers and cash back rates available to you may be personalized based on your account history, shopping behavior, and membership status, and may differ from those available to other members." The December 18, 2025 version only talked about personalizing which offers and stores you are shown, not your rate.
Neither document says what "membership status" means. The updated privacy policy does newly name one paid service, "Rakuten Plus," in its list of services that require payments.
## What Rakuten already told brands
Personalized rates are not new on Rakuten's business side. A May 14, 2024 post on Rakuten's site for brands describes "Personalized Rewards" as "tailor-made campaigns, designed to target brands' ideal audiences with a unique Cash Back rate," built on "shopper data such as brand preferences, interests, demographics, and conversion rates." It lists campaign types "including re-engagement, category affinity, and demographics targeting." In its example, a fashion brand offered new shoppers "a personalized, elevated 20% Cash Back rate, 3x the brand's typical base rate," and the post says "To ensure existing customers are not served the elevated Cash Back rate, brands have the option to layer in their own CRM data."
So the October 23 update puts in the member contract what Rakuten has pitched to brands since at least 2024: two members shopping the same store can be shown different rates. The terms don't say rates are ever lowered for anyone. They also no longer promise that everyone sees the same rate.
Two other Rakuten pages for brands, fetched November 9, 2026, show how the rates are set. Its business FAQ says "Our standard commission and Cash Back split is 50/50," and describes "Cash Back elasticity," which it calls "the term we use for strategically fluctuating Cash Back rates to meet your goals and manage margins." A case study for a luxury brand says Rakuten "launched a targeted campaign to dynamically serve two different elevated Cash Back rates, 8% and 10% respectively, alongside their 2% base rate," and that "Using our proprietary data, Rakuten targeted members who purchased within an 18-month time period." In that campaign, the same store paid some members four or five times what other members could earn.
## Why this matters now
On October 28, 2026, five days after Rakuten's update, the FTC ordered nine companies (Delta, United, JetBlue, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, Walmart and Target) to explain whether prices vary "from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data," according to The Record. Rakuten is not one of the nine. But a cash back rate is part of what you actually pay, and Rakuten's contract now says yours is set partly from your shopping behavior.
## Other changes in the October 23 terms
**Cash back becomes "Rewards," and you can convert it to partner points.** Rewards now cover cash back, Bonuses and "Partner Points" (points or other currency from partners). If you convert cash back into Partner Points, they are "issued, valued, and administered by the applicable partner under that partner's terms, including any expiration, fees, or restrictions on use, and once converted they are no longer payable by Rakuten in U.S. dollars. Conversion may not be reversible."
**Gift card limits.** You can now redeem part of your balance as gift cards, but "Gift card redemptions are subject to a maximum of $2,000 per day." A new line says Rakuten "is not responsible for any gift card that is lost, stolen, expired, or otherwise unusable after delivery."
**Forfeiture now names confirmed rewards.** In the fraud and abuse section, "forfeiture of any accrued Cash Back rewards" becomes "forfeiture of any accrued or confirmed Rewards."
**More detail on how Rakuten is paid.** Section 4 now lists "referral or affiliate fees, marketing funds, cost-per-click or other performance-based fees, commissions on gift card redemptions, and other forms of consideration," and says Rakuten funds rewards from that money "and, for some offers, from its own funds."
## How other cash back and coupon apps word it
We read the current terms of three competitors on November 9, 2026. None says outright that your rate may differ from other members' for the same store.
**PayPal Honey** (terms last updated January 16, 2024) comes closest. It says PayPal "may display to you PayPal Honey offers and other personalized and non-personalized pricing and product information," and that "Not all PayPal Honey Offers will be available on all devices, web browsers, or through all channels," which is close to Rakuten's new "by surface." It doesn't tie offers to your shopping behavior in the terms.
**Capital One Shopping** (terms effective November 5, 2026) has no language on personalized reward rates that we could find. Its terms instead let it "withhold, cancel, or subtract any pending or prior Rewards" for behavior including "engaging in a pattern of returning products or canceling services" or "accessing the Services through a VPN."
**TopCashback** (terms "most recently updated in 03 2025") says "We pass on the Cash Back we earn from merchants and their tracking agencies for your applicable transactions." Nothing in its terms says rates vary by member.
So Rakuten is, as far as we found, the only one of the big portals whose member contract now says your rate is personalized from your shopping behavior and may differ from another member's.
## What stays the same
The $5 inactivity fee is not new. Both versions say that if you haven't shopped or started a shopping trip through Rakuten for more than 12 consecutive months, Rakuten "reserves the right to debit your Account balance five dollars ($5.00) per month" until you shop again or the balance hits zero. The arbitration clause and its 30-day opt-out (by signed letter, within 30 days of joining) are also the same; only the attention line on the mailing address changed.
## What you can do
Before you click through for a big purchase, compare the rate Rakuten shows you with the rate on other cash back portals or your card's shopping portal. Comparing what you see signed in with what a signed-out browser shows is a quick check, but it is not proof of how your own rate was set.
The privacy policy (in both versions) says that when Rakuten personalizes the offers you see from your tracked behavior "for the direct benefit of a particular merchant," that may count as "selling" or "sharing," and the Section 5 opt-out "would cover and remove you from this type of targeted marketing and personalization." Rakuten also says it honors Global Privacy Control signals. Opting out may also take you out of targeted higher rates, so it can cut both ways.
If you have a balance and rarely use Rakuten, cash it out (the minimum payout is still $5.01) so the $5-a-month inactivity fee can't eat it.
Coverage (re-checked Nov 9, 2026, afternoon): We found no news story about the October 23 changes. An automated terms tracker (CrazyTOS) summarized the terms update, and one cash back review site notes the privacy line; we found nothing on how it lines up with what Rakuten tells brands.

entry.title: Booking.com price match will pay wallet credits instead of a refund (US terms, Dec 10, 2026)
entry.summary:
Booking.com has posted a US Customer Terms of Service dated 10 December 2026. It is a PDF linked from the live terms page, which is still marked "Updated August 25, 2025". We compared the two (fetched Nov 8, 2026). This is the US document; other countries may see different terms.
## Change 1: We Price Match promises wallet credits instead of a refund
The current terms say: if, after you have booked, you find the same Accommodation (with the same conditions) cheaper on another website, "we promise to refund the difference." The December 10 terms say "we promise you Wallet Credits for the difference."
The claim steps change in the same way. Both versions still say that after Booking.com validates your claim, "we will amend the reservation price (if possible)." When that is not possible, the current terms tell you how "to claim an after-stay refund of the price difference." The new terms tell you how "to claim after stay Wallet credits of the price difference."
The checklist of matching conditions is otherwise the same: same property and room type, same dates, same cancellation policy, same number of occupants, same add-on or meal plan, and the cheaper offer must be in the property's local currency and still online when they check. Loyalty-discounted, opaque, partner-offer and cancelled bookings are still excluded. Booking.com still "reserves the right to make the sole determination regarding a customer's eligibility to receive the price match."
The new clause says "Wallet Credits," not which kind. In the same document's dictionary, "Travel Credits" are a benefit you can put toward a future Travel Experience but "can't 'cash out'". "Cash Credits" can be cashed out to the payment method on file, or put toward a future trip, and the rewards section says they can be transferred to a credit or debit card of certain brands. The price-match sentence does not say you will receive Cash Credits.
## Change 2: Genius level numbers leave the contract
The current terms spell out how Genius levels work: "To reach Level 2, the user must complete 5 bookings within 2 years. To reach Level 3, the user must complete 15 bookings within 2 years." They also say "There are no membership fees, and it's easy to become a member - just create an account."
The December 10 terms drop both the numbers and the "no membership fees" sentence. They say: "It's easy to become a member - simply create an account." And: "Your Genius level is based on your booking activity on our Platform, as further explained on our Genius dedicated page."
We did not find a Genius membership fee. The Genius page (booking.com/genius.html, fetched Nov 8, 2026) still says Level 2 is unlocked "upon completing 5 bookings in 2 years" and Level 3 "upon completing 15 bookings in 2 years," and it still markets sign-up as free. What changed is that those thresholds will no longer sit in the terms themselves. Both versions already say Booking.com "may change any feature of the Genius programme, including the membership levels."
## Change 3: Identity checks, including a selfie
The current terms say: "To make a booking, you may need to create an Account." The new terms add "and/or undergo mandatory identity verification (if applicable)."
A new A9 rule says: "If you book an Accommodation which requires mandatory identity verification, We retain the right to cancel your Booking if your identity cannot be verified by one of the prescribed methods. In that case, we will cancel your booking and refund anything you've paid."
Section B also adds a Guest verification paragraph that is not in the August 2025 terms: Booking.com "may ask you to verify your identity during or after you complete your Booking, as required by the Service Provider." Methods include "your historical bookings and/or via a \"selfie\" check," and "your Booking confirmation may be subject to completion of a successful identity verification."
## Change 4: Refunds can depend on what Booking.com can recover
When Booking.com (or an affiliate) organizes your payment, the new terms add: "Any refund that you are entitled to is dependent on the amounts actually received by Us and recoverable from the Service Provider under their policy." When the Service Provider charges you directly, a new sentence says any refund "is the responsibility of and will be processed by the Service Provider."
The December 10 terms also add an Installments paragraph (A8.6). Where the option is offered, "the number of installments, interest, fees, and other conditions, are determined by the relevant payment provider, financing provider, or card issuer."
## Other changes
On Partner offers, the new terms add: "Our customer service support is limited if you book a Partner Offer." The current terms' line that a Partner offer "Can't be combined with any other offers (promotions, incentives, or rewards)" is gone.
## How this compares: practice today and Expedia
The wording change may codify what already happens. In January 2026 a r/Bookingcom user complained that an approved price match was paid into the Wallet instead of their card. A reply from the u/bookingcom account (Jan 2, 2026) said: "For We Price Match claims, compensation is provided as travel credit to your Booking.com Wallet... Once added as wallet credit, it cannot be converted back to a refund to the original payment method." (We read this through a search snapshot; Reddit blocks our server.) That is one customer's report, not proof of what every claim pays, but it is at odds with the August 25, 2025 terms ("we promise to refund the difference") and with Booking.com's We Price Match help page, which still says "You can claim a refund for the difference" (checked Nov 8).
For comparison, Expedia's own Hotel Price Guarantee page says the guarantee "will end on July 28, 2026" (eligible earlier bookings still qualify), and that before then it issued "the difference in OneKeyCash," not cash. AwardWallet and Upgraded Points both report that Expedia and Hotels.com removed it with no replacement. So Booking.com is among the few big booking sites still matching prices after booking, but from December 10 the written promise is credit, not a refund.
## What stays the same
Section A20, the arbitration agreement, is not new. The live August 25, 2025 US terms already include it, in substantially the same words: NAM arbitration, a class-action and jury waiver, a 60-day internal review step, batching of 25 or more similar claims, and a 30-day opt-out through the Dispute Resolution page with the message "Arbitration -- Opt-Out Notice." We are not treating Dec 10 as the date Booking.com added forced arbitration.
## What you can do
If you have a cheaper matching offer today, the live US terms still promise a refund of the difference, so a claim filed under those terms is the clearer path. From December 10, read the US PDF before you book, and if a price-match payout arrives as credits, check whether they are Travel Credits or Cash Credits.
Coverage (checked Nov 8, 2026): We found no news story about the December 10 US terms or the price-match wording. Wallet-credit payouts under the older wording appear only in customer posts (r/Bookingcom, Jan 2026). Automated trackers have logged Booking.com's terms, including the existing A20 arbitration clause (captured as early as Sept 19, 2026). The December 2026 PDF is linked from Booking.com's own terms page.

entry.title: JetBlue bag fees rise to $50–$85 for bookings from Nov 3, 2026 (December now all peak)
entry.summary:
JetBlue raised its checked bag fees for trips booked on or after Nov 3, 2026. We compared the live fees page (fetched Nov 7) with an archived copy from Oct 12, 2026 (Wayback Machine).
## Change 1: First and second bags cost more
For Main Base, Main, EvenMore and their Flex versions within the U.S., Latin America, the Caribbean and Canada:
- 1st bag, off-peak: $45 → $50 if you prepay at least 24 hours before departure; $49 → $60 if you pay at check-in. - 1st bag, peak: $49 → $55 prepaid; $59 → $70 at check-in. - 2nd bag, off-peak: $59 → $70 prepaid; $69 → $75 at check-in. - 2nd bag, peak: $69 → $75 prepaid; $79 → $85 at check-in.
The page lists prepaid prices with an "incl $X savings" note. The check-in price is the prepaid price plus that saving. Waiting until check-in now costs more for the first bag: the gap grew from $4 to $10 off-peak and from $10 to $15 peak. For the second bag the gap shrank from $10 to $5 off-peak and stayed at $10 peak. This is why the second-bag check-in price rose by only $6 while the prepaid price rose by $11. A 3rd or later bag is still $200.
The same higher second-bag fees apply to Mosaic 1 members, JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders, and the new BlueFirst Base and Mint Base fares, even though their first bag is free.
## Change 2: December is now all peak
In the Oct 12 copy, peak dates were Nov 19–30 and Dec 17–31, 2026. The live page adds Nov 5–11 and makes all of December peak (12/1–12/31). Peak runs on into Jan 1–18, 2027, and the calendar now reaches October 2027. Here is the combined effect. Say you book a trip now that flies in early-to-mid December, with one prepaid bag each way. Those dates were off-peak, so the bags cost $90 ($45 × 2). Now they cost $110 ($55 × 2). With two bags each way, the cost rises from $208 to $260.
## Change 3: Transatlantic bags go up too
For Main Base and EvenMore Base on transatlantic flights, the first bag rises from $75 to $80 off-peak and from $85 to $90 peak. The second bag rises from $109 to $115 off-peak and from $119 to $125 peak, for all fares that pay for one. The pound and euro prices went up by similar amounts.
## What stays the same
The refund rule is not new. The Oct 12 copy has the same sentence: "checked bag fees are only refundable if the entire booking is cancelled prior to scheduled departure." You can still pay for bags with TrueBlue points before check-in. Mint, BlueFirst (non-Base), and Mosaic 2–4 members still get two free bags.
## Bookings made before Nov 3
The page now says: "For bookings made prior to 11/3, check Manage Trips for applicable baggage fees." The Points Guy reports that the previous fees apply to flights bought before Nov 3. JetBlue's page does not say whether those bookings use the old peak calendar, so check Manage Trips for your own trip.
## What JetBlue says
The Points Guy reported that JetBlue pointed to rising fuel and operating costs. A spokesperson said: "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
## A number we couldn't match
The Points Guy says the off-peak prepaid first bag was "up from $39" and calls $50 "a 28% jump". Our archived Oct 12 copy of JetBlue's own page shows $45 (incl $4 savings). TPG's figures for paying at check-in ($49 before, $60 after) match the page. We use JetBlue's archived page for the before prices. Measured from $45, the prepaid first-bag fee rose 11%.
Coverage (checked Nov 7, 2026): The Points Guy (Nov 3) reported the increase as JetBlue's second bag-fee hike of 2026. We could not load AP's article (it was blocked by a bot check).

entry.title: BeReal privacy policy (Nov 3, 2026): 5-year inactivity deletion, new ad measurement partners and store-visit tracking
entry.summary:
BeReal updated its Privacy Policy. The live page says "Last updated: November 3, 2026." Our previous copy (archived Sept 30, 2026) said "Last updated: June 30, 2026." Two things changed in substance.
## Change 1: Inactive accounts are kept for five years
Before, an unused account "may be deleted" after three years of inactivity in the U.S. and after two years in Europe and everywhere else. Now there is one rule for everyone: five years. BeReal says the longer period exists because it keeps your posts as a personal archive (Memories) "so that you can find it again whenever you come back to the App." The phrase "To minimize data retention" was removed from both sentences where it appeared. Inactivity still runs from your "most recent login or connection to the App."
The warning is now firmer. The old text said BeReal "may send you a prior notice via text message (SMS)". The new text says "Before your account is deleted, BeReal will send you a prior notice." It still goes only by text message to the phone number on the account. If you have changed numbers, you may never see it.
In practice, a European user who stopped opening BeReal in late 2024 would have faced deletion under the old two-year rule. Under the new rule, their photos stay on BeReal's servers until about 2029 unless they delete them.
## Change 2: A new kind of ad partner, and store-visit measurement
Section 3 adds "Advertising measurement partners" as a new kind of third party. These partners process data "under their own control". BeReal "may share mobile advertising IDs, device identifiers and advertising-exposure data" with them. The uses are app-install attribution and, "where you agree, visits to physical locations following advertising exposure." The ad-measurement row in Section 2 now covers "attributing app installs and other conversions". It adds Geolocation Data (location inferred from your IP address) and advertising-exposure data, and says visit results are "provided to us in aggregated form."
## What the consent wording does and doesn't say
- "Where you agree" applies only to the store-visit measurement. The row as a whole, including install attribution and sharing your ad ID, still relies on "Your consent, where required by applicable law; otherwise, our legitimate interest." Outside places that legally require consent, BeReal does not promise to ask first. - "Aggregated form" describes what BeReal gets back. It does not describe what partners receive. They get device-level IDs and advertising-exposure data, and the policy does not say how they decide that a visit happened. - The in-app consent instructions were not updated. "Modify my consents" is still described as covering Ad Partners and the use of machine learning on your photos. It does not mention measurement partners by name, so we can't confirm from the policy that a separate toggle exists. - U.S. section 9.4 already listed "Advertising and measurement partners" in the June version. What's new is the Section 3 category and the store-visit purpose, not the U.S. disclosure category.
## Who the "measurement partners" are
The new paragraph says you "will find a list of our partners" via a link. That link goes to the same Ad Partners page in BeReal's Help Center that the existing Ad Partners paragraph uses (help.bereal.com, checked Nov 7, 2026). It lists 93 companies: ad exchanges, ad networks and demand-side platforms such as Google Ad Manager, Meta, Amazon, AppLovin, The Trade Desk and Vistar Media. None is marked as a measurement partner. The page doesn't name the mobile attribution firms such as AppsFlyer, Adjust, Branch, Kochava or Singular, or any company that does store-visit measurement. So from the published list you can't tell which company would work out whether you visited a store.
## How five years compares
Google's inactive-account policy lets it delete a personal Google Account after at least two years of inactivity across Google (support.google.com, checked Nov 7, 2026). BeReal used to sit close to that, at two years in Europe and three in the U.S. It now waits more than twice as long. BeReal's own justification is the Memories archive. The old policy gave a different reason for its shorter periods: "To minimize data retention." That phrase is gone.
## What stays the same
Interest inference from your photos and gender inference from your profile, for internal ad targeting, are unchanged. So are hashed phone-number matching for advertisers, the UX recording of 0.001% of users, the 15-day account deletion grace period and the 10-year retention of transaction records.
Coverage (checked again Nov 7, 2026, afternoon): we did not find an announcement from BeReal or any press coverage of this update. Only automated policy trackers (TermsWatch, which draws on Open Terms Archive) logged it.

entry.title: Proton doubles free-account inactivity window from 12 to 24 months (Nov 2026)

The Oct 20, 2026 rewrite still stands: advance warnings at 30, 15 and 7 days are only "a mere courtesy" Proton will "aim" to send to the recovery email. That did not get any firmer today. There is also no new effective-date stamp on the page in our snapshot; the wording is live in today's capture.
## Leftover inconsistency
One sentence further down still says that if "insurmountable circumstances" keep you from staying active "in a period of 12 months," you should contact Customer Support so they can prevent deletion. The main rule above it now says 24 months. We are logging the wording as it appears; the support-request line looks like it was not updated with the rest.
## How it compares
This is a rare consumer-friendly terms edit. Most inactivity policies we track tighten or add "courtesy" language. Proton already had the courtesy-only warnings; today it gave free users another year of runway.

entry.title: Wells Fargo AI Agent terms (Nov 24, 2026): Section 15 explained
entry.summary:
Wells Fargo is adding a brand-new Section 15, "Third-Party Artificial Intelligence Agents or Agentic AI," to its Online Access Agreement, the contract that covers its website and mobile app. The upcoming text is marked "Version Effective November 24, 2026." The version in force today, dated May 21, 2026, has no AI agent section and does not use the term "AI Agent" anywhere. Wells Fargo's customer notice says "You don't need to take any action" and that if you keep using online or mobile banking after November 24, 2026, "the updated Agreement applies."
## Change 1: A definition wide enough to cover a script
Section 15(a) defines an AI Agent as "any software, application, program, or other technology that takes autonomous, semi-autonomous, or non-autonomous action on behalf of any person or entity." The word "non-autonomous" is the one to notice. Read literally, the definition isn't limited to chatbots or AI shopping assistants; it can reach ordinary automation, such as a script that signs in to download statements, a budgeting app that logs in with your username and password, or a browser extension or password manager that fills in and submits forms for you. The section applies if you "use, allow, enable, or authorize" any such tool "to access, use, or interact with any Service or any Eligible Account."
## Change 2: What an agent does counts as you
Under Section 15(d), if you give an agent access "using your login credentials, or otherwise authorize an AI Agent to act on your behalf," then "Any instructions, actions, or transactions initiated by the AI Agent are deemed to have been initiated and authorized directly by you, without further verification." Wells Fargo adds that it has "no obligation to investigate, verify, or confirm the authority, authenticity, or validity of any instruction or action taken by an AI Agent."
Section 15(e) says "Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK." It makes you "solely responsible" for, among other things, "unintended actions performed by the AI Agent, actions resulting from incomplete, inaccurate, or manipulated inputs, or the AI Agent exceeding the authority granted by you." That covers an agent that misreads you, one that is tricked by a malicious web page or email (prompt injection), and one that goes further than you asked. Wells Fargo also says: "we do not monitor, screen, or review AI Agent activities, including any transactions initiated by an AI Agent." Section 15(d) and the last item in 15(e) both start with "Unless otherwise provided by law or regulation," so protections the law gives you still come first. The agreement doesn't say which ones.
## Change 3: You consent to sharing, and Wells Fargo's privacy rules stop at the agent
Section 15(c): "you acknowledge and expressly consent to the sharing of your financial, account, and personal information with such AI Agent." Section 15(b) adds that "our privacy and security policies do not apply to any AI Agent" and that Wells Fargo has "no responsibility for, and no control over, how any third party or AI Agent collects, uses, reuses, stores, shares, or protects your data."
## Change 4: To revoke an agent, keep proof and tell the bank
Section 15(f): "You are responsible for properly and timely revoking any authorization provided to an AI Agent and taking any necessary further action to cease the AI Agent’s activities. You must retain evidence of such revocation and must provide such evidence to us, at our request. Until you notify us of such revocation pursuant to Section 17(d), you remain responsible for all the AI Agent’s activities, to the extent permitted by law or regulation."
Section 17(d), "Protecting Your Security," lists two ways to notify Wells Fargo: "Call 1-800-956-4442 anytime, 24 hours a day, seven days a week" or "Write to Wells Fargo Customer Correspondence, PO Box 6995, Portland, OR, 97228-6995." Section 17(d) itself is about lost passwords, compromised devices and suspected fraud; it doesn't mention AI agents. The agreement also doesn't say what counts as "evidence of such revocation."
## Change 5: Registration, blocking, and an 18+ rule
Section 15(g) lets Wells Fargo change its rules for agents "at any time," "including requiring that you register your AI Agents with us." It may also "Change, limit, restrict, or discontinue any application programming interface (API) or other access method for AI Agents" and "Limit, prohibit, prevent, suspend, or terminate access by any AI Agent to the Service or any Eligible Account." If that breaks a tool you rely on, "we are not responsible for any resulting impact." Section 15(h) adds an age rule: "you will not permit any AI Agent to access or use the Service or any Eligible Account on your behalf if you are under 18 years of age."
## Change 6: Your Delegates' agents, indemnity and security procedures
Outside Section 15, the new terms add AI agents to clauses that already existed in the May 21 version.
Section 2: transactions by an Authorized Representative or Delegate "(including the transactions of their AI Agents)" count as authorized by you, and "You are solely responsible for supervising all of your Authorized Representatives and Delegates (including their AI Agents)." So if someone you've given access to plugs their own agent into your account, you carry that too.
Section 20(c), indemnification: you already agree to cover Wells Fargo's costs for third-party claims tied to use of the Service. That now applies whether the use was "by you, your Authorized Representative, or your Delegate (or by any of the AI Agents of such persons)."
Sections 8(b) (online wire transfers) and 17(c) (other transfers under UCC Article 4A, "including online transactions from business accounts") each add: "If you permit an AI Agent or other third party access to the Service, you acknowledge that doing so may adversely impact the commercially reasonable security procedures that you've otherwise agreed to, and you accept the risk of such access." That matters because under 8(b) you already "agree to be bound by any Order that Wells Fargo receives and verifies following the Security Procedure, even if the Order was not authorized by you."
## What you can do
Read Section 15 of the upcoming agreement before November 24, 2026. If you don't need an agent or automation tool signed in to Wells Fargo, don't give it your username and password. If one already has access, revoke it at the provider, change your Wells Fargo password if the tool had it, save a dated screenshot or confirmation of the revocation, and then call 1-800-956-4442 or write to the Portland PO box above so the notice required by Section 15(f) is on record. Note the date, time and who you spoke to. If you have Delegates, ask whether they use AI tools on your accounts.
## What stays the same
Wells Fargo isn't banning third-party agents. Section 15 sets the terms for using them and reserves the right to restrict them later. Nothing changes before November 24, 2026. The customer summary also lists other updates (newer security features, email notices for online statements, Paze information sharing in Section 10(c), which is already in the May 21 version, an expanded Eligible Accounts definition, and terms for ExpressSend Mobile and Smart Start Banking). None of those is the main change here.
## How this compares: Chase's Terms of Use
Chase's public Terms of Use (chase.com/digital/resources/terms-of-use, checked Nov 6, 2026) also has an "AI Agent or Agentic AI Notices" section, but it draws a narrower line. Chase defines an AI Agent as software or a service that "takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action" — it does not say "non-autonomous." Chase tells agents they must identify themselves as AI, "clearly and deterministically label all agentic traffic," and answer truthfully when asked whether a human or an agent is interacting. It also says unauthorized use of its systems includes using AI agents "designed to circumvent any restriction, condition, or technological measure that controls access." On responsibility, Chase says that when you deploy an AI Agent, "you are responsible for any actions or errors that may result from the Agent's incorrect interpretation or implementation of your instructions, if it performs unintended actions or exceeds the authority you gave it."
Wells Fargo's upcoming Section 15 goes further in several places Chase's Terms of Use do not: it includes "non-autonomous" action in the definition; it requires you to retain evidence of revocation and stay responsible until you notify the bank under Section 17(d); it reserves the right to require you to register AI Agents; it bars people under 18 from permitting an AI Agent on their behalf; and it folds Delegates' AI Agents into authorization, indemnification and security-procedure risk language elsewhere in the Online Access Agreement. American Banker and others have also reported that Chase's separate Digital Services Agreement (effective Oct 27, 2026) takes a different posture again — prohibiting credential-based third-party access while assigning liability if customers share logins anyway. We are quoting Chase's live Terms of Use page here because that is the primary text we could re-fetch today; the Digital Services Agreement is behind account login for us.
Coverage (re-checked Nov 6, 2026 PM): Penny Crosman's Nov 2 American Banker piece broke the prove-you-revoked / stay-liable angle. The National Law Review compared big-bank blocks vs Wells Fargo's permit-at-your-risk approach. Captain Compliance (Nov 3) walked through Section 15 in depth, including the non-autonomous definition, registration, and a Chase Digital Services Agreement comparison, plus Regulation E questions. ACA International and TokenPost largely follow those reports. We have not found news coverage that focuses on the under-18 ban in Section 15(h), the Delegates / Section 20(c) indemnification / Sections 8(b) and 17(c) security-procedure stack, or a full blackline against the May 21, 2026 agreement (which has zero "AI Agent" mentions). This article keeps those angles and the primary-document quotes.

entry.title: Smule terms and privacy update (Dec 4, 2026): AI training, licensing recordings, 18+ age limit
entry.summary:
Smule, the karaoke and social singing app, has posted a new Terms of Service and Privacy Policy that take effect December 4, 2026. They replace terms last updated September 28, 2023 and a privacy policy updated April 10, 2025. Smule announced the update in a November 4 blog post. We compared the new documents with the current ones.
Change 1: Your recordings can train Smule's AI. The new terms add, inside the license you already give Smule over what you post: "We may use and retain Personal Information and User Content to develop, train, test, and improve the artificial intelligence and machine learning models and features that power our own Services, and we may license or otherwise make available De-Identified Data to Recording Licensees, including to develop, train, test, improve, and commercialize artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, models and features." The privacy policy gives examples of Smule's own uses: "such as providing recommendations and pitch and range feedback in Coach." Smule's blog says: "Content used for Smule’s own AI training stays linked to your account, and access to it is limited." The current privacy policy and terms don't mention AI or machine learning at all.
Change 2: De-identified recordings can be licensed to other companies to build AI. The current privacy policy says only: "In limited situations, we share de-identified content and information with researchers for educational research purposes." The new one says: "We may share or license De-Identified Data with or to Recording Licensees, including to develop, train, test, improve, and commercialize artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, models and features." Smule's blog lists example uses: separating vocals from instrumentals, coaching and performance feedback, cleaning up audio, pitch correction and music discovery, and says "These are examples, not a complete list." Smule says it seeks contractual commitments requiring licensees "not to attempt to re-identify you, not to use the recordings to create a voiceprint or faceprint or to otherwise identify any individual." The blog says that before content is licensed, Smule removes "personal details such as your username, email address, and device ID." The policy doesn't name any licensees.
Change 3: It covers recordings you already shared, and the opt-out can't undo anything. The blog answers "Does this apply to recordings I’ve already shared?" with "Yes." For licensing, the new policy says: "Your opt-out applies to all of your User Content, including User Content you posted before opting out, but applies only to De-Identified Data we make available after we process your opt-out. It does not affect De-Identified Data provided to Recording Licensees before then, consistent with applicable law." For Smule's own AI training, "your opt out applies to go-forward processing only and may not undo or otherwise affect processing completed prior to our receipt of your opt out."
Change 4: The opt-out switch only opens on December 4. Smule's summary of changes says: "Beginning on December 4, 2026, you may opt out of Smule’s AI training, our licensing of de-identified data to third parties, or both, in the Smule app or on smule.com under Settings > Privacy > AI & Data, or through our online support form." That's the same day the new terms take effect. Before then, the only alternative Smule offers is to leave: "If you do not agree to the updated Terms, you may delete your account in the Smule app (Settings > Support > Delete Account) or through our online support form prior to December 4, 2026." The two opt-outs are separate, and the policy says they apply "to all users regardless of location."
Change 5: Under-18s are out. The current terms say "TO USE THE SERVICE, YOU MUST BE AT LEAST 13 YEARS OF AGE" in the US (16 in most of the EEA, 18 in several countries). The new terms say "TO USE THE SERVICE, YOU MUST BE AT LEAST 18 YEARS OF AGE." The new privacy policy adds: "If we become aware that a minor under the Minimum Age has an account, we take steps to suspend or terminate the minor’s account." It doesn't say whether teens get a chance to download their recordings first.
Change 6: Arbitration opt-out moves to mail only, and the right to reject future arbitration changes is gone. The current terms let you opt out of arbitration "no later than thirty (30) days after first registering to use the Service," by mail or through an online link. The new terms require written notice "postmarked within thirty (30) days of first accepting these Terms" to a Salt Lake City address. They don't say whether existing users get a fresh 30 days when the new terms start. The current terms also say that if Smule changes the arbitration clause later, "you may reject the change by sending Smule written notice within thirty (30) days of the change." That sentence isn't in the new terms. The new version says Smule "will pay all arbitration fees for claims less than seventy-five thousand ($75,000) dollars."
What did not change. Smule says: "We do not use your User Content to create a voiceprint to identify you." The license you grant Smule over your posted content was already perpetual and sublicensable, and the current terms already call it irrevocable to the extent the law allows. The new privacy policy also notes that because voice and video recordings can count as biometric data under some state laws, "certain content you provide may constitute Sensitive Personal Data under certain U.S. State Privacy Laws."
How this compares: SoundCloud went the other way. In May 2025, after artists spotted a line added to its terms in 2024 saying uploads "may be used to inform, train, develop or serve as input to artificial intelligence or machine intelligence technologies or services," SoundCloud said it would replace it (reported by The Verge and Music Business Worldwide). Its terms now say: "We will not use your content to train generative AI models that aim to replicate or synthesize your voice, music, or likeness without your explicit consent, which must be affirmatively provided through an opt-in mechanism." Smule's new terms work the opposite way: AI training and licensing apply to everyone's recordings unless you opt out, and the opt-out only opens on December 4. Smule's new terms and privacy policy also don't say anything either way about generative AI or voice cloning. The words "generative," "synthesize" and "clone" don't appear in either document. The limits on licensees are about identity (no re-identifying users, no voiceprints or faceprints), and Smule's blog calls its list of example uses "examples, not a complete list."
What you can do: On or after December 4, go to Settings > Privacy > AI & Data and turn off AI training, licensing, or both. If you'd rather your recordings never reach either use, the only option before December 4 is deleting your account, and deleting doesn't undo uses that already happened. Teens, and parents of teens, should save any recordings they want before December 4.
Coverage (checked again the afternoon of Nov 5, 2026): We found no news coverage. The only mentions we found were Smule's own blog post, a repost of it on a Smule fan forum, and a few user posts on X.
