entry.title: SSA SSN master file (60-0058): new Treasury Do Not Pay routine use, comments due Dec 3, 2026
entry.summary:
The Social Security Administration published a notice in the November 3, 2026 Federal Register (FR Doc. 2026-22356, docket SSA-2026-0760) modifying its system of records called Master Files of Social Security Number (SSN) Holders and SSN Applications (60-0058), last published February 20, 2025. This is the file SSA uses to assign SSNs and that holds a record of each person who applied for and was assigned one: application details such as name, date and place of birth, sex, parents' names and alien registration number, plus citizenship or work-authorization codes and fraud indicators.
Change 1: a new routine use. SSA adds one new routine use (No. 48) allowing it to disclose records to the Department of the Treasury to review SSA's payment and award eligibility through the Do Not Pay Working System, for identifying, preventing or recouping improper payments. SSA says it applies only when the disclosure meets the requirements in 20 CFR 401.150(c). The new routine use takes effect December 3, 2026.
Change 2: more record sources. SSA expands where the file's information comes from to include Federal contractors and vendors and other SSA systems such as the Claims Folders System (60-0089) and the Master Beneficiary Record (60-0090).
Other changes: SSA clarifies the system location and system manager, rewrites routine uses 6, 7, 10, 12, 17, 25 and 45 for readability, deletes routine use 2 as duplicative, and fixes formatting and typos. SSA says it republished the whole notice for ease of reference. The rest of the notice is applicable on publication.
What you can do: send comments by December 3, 2026 through regulations.gov (docket SSA-2026-0760) or by mail to SSA's Head of Privacy and Disclosure Policy.
Why it matters: this is not a new database. It is an expanded list of who SSA may share the SSN file with, published days after SSA announced a separate Client Data System that combines 12 record systems into one profile per SSN.

entry.title: Stripe privacy policy update (effective Nov 20, 2026): AI voice agents, data to card issuers
entry.summary:
Stripe, the company whose payment forms sit behind a huge share of online checkouts, posted a preview of a rewritten Privacy Policy that takes effect November 20, 2026. The policy in force today is dated April 28, 2026. A notice at the top of stripe.com/privacy says the policy "will be updated on November 20, 2026," and links to the preview. We compared the preview with the current policy sentence by sentence. Stripe's own summary of the update lists "automated dialing, AI voice agents, and transcripts for outreach and model training," but the rewrite also adds several lines that reach people who only ever used a Stripe-powered checkout.
Change 1: AI voice agents may call you, and the calls can train AI. A new "Automated and AI-Powered Communications" paragraph says: "We may leverage automated dialing systems and AI technologies, such as AI-powered voice agents and AI transcription, chat, and email tools, to initiate and conduct communications with you for operational, support, sales, marketing, and lead qualification purposes." It adds that Stripe may use "call recordings and transcripts of interactions facilitated by automated systems for staff training, quality assurance, and other operational purposes, as well as to train, test, and improve the artificial intelligence and machine learning models." The only opt-out it offers is for recording: "To opt out of call recording, please do so when prompted at the beginning of the call." Stripe's existing AI-training line, "Training artificial intelligence models to power our Services and protect against fraud and other harm," now ends "and for other internal training, quality assurance, and operational improvement purposes."
Change 2: Your IP address, email, phone and shipping address may go to your card's bank. The new text says: "During payment authorization, Stripe may also share fraud risk signals—including Stripe's risk assessment, and your IP address, email address, phone number, and shipping address—with your card-issuing bank to help approve genuine transactions and reduce unnecessary payment failures. Card issuers are independent data controllers for signals they receive." The words "card-issuing bank" and that list of fields do not appear in the April policy.
Change 3: Your payments at one store can shape how Stripe handles you at another. New: "Stripe uses transaction signals pooled across its global merchant network to optimize payment authorization rates. This means transaction patterns from your payments at one merchant may inform how Stripe routes authorization requests at other merchants."
Change 4: Tracking at signup and login, before you pay. New: "Stripe's fraud detection services may collect device and behavioral signals at the time of account registration and login on platforms that have enabled Stripe's risk API services. These signals are used to detect multi-account abuse and fraudulent registrations before a payment is initiated. Merchants using these services are required by their Stripe agreement to disclose this collection to their customers."
Change 5: Abandoned-checkout emails. New: "If you begin a checkout session on a Stripe-powered payment page and enter your email address but do not complete the purchase, the merchant may instruct Stripe to send you a recovery email as a reminder." The opt-out is the email's unsubscribe link or asking the merchant. The policy also newly discloses tracking pixels in some Stripe emails that show "whether an email has been opened and which links within the email have been clicked."
Change 6: Your Link purchase data may be used for "insights" shown to businesses. New: "Where permitted by applicable law, and where required with your consent or other notice requirements, we may use your Transaction Data with your Link account (where one is available) to derive insights, personalize offers and communications, and make them available to Business Users." The opt-out is "managing applicable data-sharing and advertising preferences through your Link Settings." Stripe also says Link moves to "a separate Link Privacy Policy."
Change 7: Payments made by AI agents. Stripe adds a stated purpose of "Facilitating, authenticating, processing, supporting, and protecting transactions initiated through AI agents, automated software, or other authorized third-party services, including managing related payment credentials, tokens, authorizations, refunds, disputes, and transaction-related requests." The rewrite also adds stablecoin and blockchain transactions.
Change 8: The privacy-signal opt-out gets narrower. The April policy says in one line: "Stripe honors the Global Privacy Control (GPC) opt-out preference signals." The new version says Stripe will honor a GPC signal "as a request to opt out of 'sales' and 'sharing' (for behavioral advertising) for the device and associated browser that transmits the signal," and adds: "if you or your browser clear or expire cookies, you will need to opt-out or transmit a Global Privacy Control signal again to opt-out." Stripe's policy also still says its provision of data to some third parties "may be considered a data 'sale' or 'sharing' (for behavioral advertising)" under California and other US privacy laws.
What did not change. Stripe still says "We do not share mobile data we collect for authentication purposes with third parties for marketing or promotional purposes." It still says it does not sell or share sensitive personal information. Call recording was already in the April policy.
What you can do: Before November 20, nothing is required of you. If you don't want Stripe's outreach calls recorded, say so when the call starts. Unsubscribe from any abandoned-cart email. If you have a Link account, review the data-sharing and advertising settings at app.link.com/settings. Turn on Global Privacy Control in your browser and expect to re-send it if you clear cookies. To ask what Stripe holds about you, use the contact route in the policy (privacy@stripe.com).
Coverage (checked Nov 3, 2026): We found no news coverage. The only mentions we found were an automated policy-tracker blog post (Venpo, Oct 23), which is aimed at businesses that use Stripe, and a LinkedIn post about Stripe's notice email.

entry.title: Calm privacy policy and terms change (Oct 13, 2026): health inferences, AI features
entry.summary:
Calm, the meditation and sleep app, updated both its Privacy Policy and its Terms of Service with the same date: "Last Updated: October 13, 2026." The privacy policy it replaced was dated December 12, 2024. We compared the new US terms with the July 10, 2025 US terms in an Internet Archive capture from December 26, 2025; we can't rule out a version in between. Calm didn't announce either update on its site or blog that we could find.
Change 1: Calm may now infer health traits from how you say you feel. The privacy policy's "Views and opinions" section used to say: "Some users also provide information about how they are feeling in connection with providing feedback or other messages to us, but we do not infer any health-related characteristics from this information and only process it consistent with the purpose for which it was provided." It now says: "Some users also provide information about how they are feeling in connection with providing feedback or other messages to us; we may infer health-related characteristics from this information but will only process it consistent with the purpose for which it was provided." The sentence covers feedback and messages you send Calm. The separate line about Apple Health and Health Connect data still says "we do not infer any health-related characteristics" from it.
Change 2: New terms for AI features. The terms add an "Artificial Intelligence Features" section. It says "Calm and its third-party service providers may process any User Content, and any other information, prompts, queries, inputs or materials submitted by you to the AI Features." It also says "Certain AI Features may allow you to submit information regarding your emotions, well-being, stress levels, personal experiences, goals, or other wellness-related matters," and that this information "may be processed by the AI Features to generate personalized Outputs and improve your experience with the Services." It adds: "You are not required to provide sensitive personal information to use the Services or any AI Feature." And: "If potential abuse or violations of these Terms are detected, Calm may log Inputs and Outputs solely for the purpose of reviewing and determining whether a violation has occurred." The privacy policy separately adds: "We may process your information for any of the above purposes, including through the help of automated technology vendors."
Change 3: A wider license to what you post, now including AI output. The July 2025 terms gave Calm a license to your User Content "in connection with operating, marketing, and providing the Services." The new terms cover "your User Content or Outputs" and the purpose is now "operating, providing, maintaining, securing, supporting, marketing, developing, testing, validating, enhancing, and improving the Services and related products and services."
Change 4: Your Premium library is a rental. A new "Access to Calm Premium Content" section says Paid Content "is a limited, personal, revocable license that lasts only while your subscription or other required payment is active. You do not own or acquire any permanent rights in Paid Content. This applies even to Paid Content you have downloaded or saved to a device; downloaded content is licensed for offline use only while your access is active and may become unavailable automatically once it ends." It adds: "We may add, change, or remove Paid Content at any time, and specific titles or features may become unavailable even while your subscription is active."
Change 5: Ad sharing spelled out, and a new line for minors. A new section for residents of specific US states says: "We 'share' and 'sell' identifiers and electronic network activity with our advertising partners (including social media platforms) so our advertising partners can show ads that are targeted to your interests on other platforms." It says Calm will only sell or share sensitive personal information with consent and doesn't sell sensitive data, including consumer health data, of residents of states that prohibit it, such as Maryland. The December 2024 policy already said its ad tracking "may be considered 'sales,' 'sharing,' or 'targeted advertising.'" New and in users' favor: "We do not knowingly process the personal data of a user for targeted advertising, or sell such data, where we know or should know the user is under 18."
Other changes: The terms add a "Scope of Services" section saying "Calm is not a healthcare provider, mental health provider, therapist, counselor, psychologist, psychiatrist, medical practice, or crisis-response service." They also ban using Calm "to develop any product or artificial intelligence model that competes with the Services," add rules for inviting friends, and extend your indemnity to the AI features.
How it compares (policy read Nov 2, 2026): Headspace's privacy policy, effective October 28, 2026, has no line about inferring health traits from feelings you share in messages; the only place it uses the word "infer" is in its definition of artificial intelligence. It does say of health information shared with coaches or therapists: "We understand that this information is very sensitive so we handle it with care, including treating this health information as protected health information under HIPAA where applicable." The two apps aren't identical, because Headspace sells coaching and therapy and Calm says in its new terms that it is not a healthcare provider, but the difference shows where Calm's wording sits.
Calm Health gets the same wording. Calm Health, the version of Calm offered through employers, health plans and other sponsors, has its own privacy policy, also "last updated October 13, 2026" (its terms are dated October 14). Its "Views and opinions" line is identical: "we may infer health-related characteristics from this information." That policy also lists health information Calm Health collects, such as survey answers about your "current mental or physical health status," and says that if a sponsor gives you access, Calm collects information that "may include health information" to enroll you. It points to a separate Calm Health Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy for details.
What stays the same: Disputes still go to individual arbitration with JAMS (now section 17). New users can still opt out by emailing notices@calm.com "within thirty (30) days following the date you first agree to these Terms."
What you can do: Opt out of ad "sales" and "sharing" at calm.com/optout, or turn on Global Privacy Control in your browser. On your phone, turn off app tracking (iOS: Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking). If you'd rather Calm not draw health conclusions from what you write, keep feelings out of feedback, support messages and any AI chat. To ask what Calm holds about you or to delete it, email support@calm.com.
Coverage (checked Nov 2, 2026): We found no news coverage of either update. The only other mention we found was an automated policy tracker.

entry.title: Tubi privacy policy change (Oct 22, 2026): Fox policy, precise location, teen ad age 16
entry.summary:
Tubi, the free ad-supported streaming service Fox has owned since 2020, replaced its own privacy policy on October 22, 2026. The page at tubitv.com/static/privacy now shows the joint policy of "Fox Digital Services, LLC, along with Fox News, Fox Sports, Fox Broadcasting Company, Tubi, Inc., and Fox Television Stations (collectively "Company" or "we")", dated "Last Updated/Effective Date: October 22, 2026." Fox News' privacy policy page carries the same date. We compared it with Tubi's previous standalone policy, dated July 1, 2026, as captured by the Internet Archive on October 20, 2026. Tubi published the change without a summary.
Change 1: precise location. The July policy said: "In certain circumstances, we also may collect general location information, such as the city, state, and country where the device is located." The same sentence now reads: "In certain circumstances, we also may collect geolocation data (including your precise location)." Fox's own July policy already used that wording. In the California table, the category "Non-Precise Geolocation data" is renamed "Geolocation data, such as device location." To be fair to Tubi, the new tables also mark location as not sold or shared ("N/A") and no longer list "To deliver relevant advertisements" as a purpose for it. The July tables listed non-precise location as sold or shared with "Advertising technology companies; advertisers" for targeted advertising. So Tubi now reserves the right to collect more exact location, but says it doesn't pass location to ad companies.
Change 2: teen protection drops from 18 to 16 in some states. In the section for residents of US states with privacy laws other than California, the July policy said Tubi does not knowingly sell, or process for targeted advertising, the personal data "of minors known to be under 18 years of age" in states whose laws prohibit it. The new policy says "under 16 years of age." The California section's under-16 line is unchanged.
Change 3: AI tools and inferences. A new line says the company "may use artificial intelligence (AI) tools in connection with some of the Company Services, for example, to help provide customer support (e.g., chatbots) or to provide advertising and content that you may find more relevant and interesting." Profiling is now a stated purpose of its own. July said Tubi personalizes content and ads "(including, in certain circumstances, by making predictions and inferences about your interests)". The new policy lists, as a use, "to make inferences and predictions about your potential areas of interest in order to provide you with content and advertising that is more interesting, personalized, and relevant to you."
Change 4: data shared across Fox and with subscription partners. "Tubi Affiliates" become "Company Affiliates", the same group that runs Fox News, Fox Sports and Fox's TV stations, and they are now listed as receiving data "For the purpose of marketing, personalization, and targeted advertising" (July: "marketing and targeted advertising"). "Providers of streaming subscriptions" are added as recipients, along with a new use: "If you choose to purchase, request, or redeem a subscription from or through another party, we may process and share information about you, such as your email address, to facilitate subscriptions with or through that company."
Other changes: registration information now lists "phone number" and "birthday" (July: "account name, email address, gender, zip code, and age"). The Social Engagement Features text (following, re-posting and reacting, and public profile information) is gone. Kids' information moved out of the main policy. The new policy says it doesn't apply to Tubi Kids Accounts and Tubi Kids Mode for children under 13, and those are covered by a separate Children's Privacy Policy, also dated October 22, 2026.
How it compares (policies read Nov 1, 2026): precise location in a privacy policy is normal for big ad-supported streamers. Roku's privacy policy (last updated July 1, 2026) lists "Precise geolocation" as a category it collects. NBCUniversal's policy, which covers Peacock (last updated November 17, 2025), says "We will ask for your permission before using your precise location from GPS-based functionality on your mobile devices," and lists "displaying an ad relevant to your precise location data" as an example of how it may use sensitive data for targeted advertising. Paramount Skydance's policy, which Pluto TV links to (last modified May 12, 2026), says it uses precise location information to, among other things, "serve you targeted advertising." So Tubi has caught up with its peers on collecting precise location, while its new tables say location isn't sold or shared with advertisers. On teens, 16 is a common line: Roku and Paramount both say they have no actual knowledge of selling or sharing the data of people under 16, which matches California's under-16 rule. But Paramount's separate Minors' Privacy Policy (last modified April 21, 2026) goes further: "If you are under 18 and are using our services that have advertisements, we only show you advertisements that make sense for the type of shows you are watching," meaning contextual ads, not targeted ones. Tubi's July policy made an under-18 promise for state-law states; the new one stops at 16.
What you can do: Tubi's opt-out form for the sale or sharing of data for targeted advertising is still at tubitv.com/privacy/opt-out. Your device's location permission controls whether the Tubi app can get precise location at all.
Coverage (checked Nov 1, 2026): web, news and X searches found no reporting on the change. An automated terms tracker logged a Tubi update on October 23.

entry.title: Toyota privacy notice update (Oct 28, 2026): personal data used to train large language models, Acxiom tracking
entry.summary:
Toyota Motor North America updated two US privacy notices on October 28, 2026: the general Toyota Privacy Notice that covers toyota.com, the Toyota app, call-center contacts and dealer-related records, and the Toyota Connected Services Privacy Notice that covers data sent from connected vehicles. Both now carry the date "Updated as of: October 28, 2026." We compared the general notice with the July 1, 2026 version recorded by Open Terms Archive, and the Connected Services notice with the July 1, 2026 PDF that is still posted on toyota.com. Toyota published the changes without a summary.
Change 1: training large language models is now a listed use of your personal information. In the July version of the general notice, large language models came up only in the definition of "Research Data," which Toyota described as data "related to Toyota’s consumer and product research," such as "your responses to surveys, insights generated from simulated user profiles, and information you provide as part of a focus group." The October 28 version adds a separate line to section 3, "How We Use The Personal Information We Collect": "For the purpose of training large language models." That list covers the personal information Toyota collects "about and from you," which the notice says includes contact details, vehicle ownership and service records, website and app activity, and "call center records and screen, audio and/or video recordings."
Change 2: the connected-car notice says it outright. The July Connected Services notice already listed "Artificial intelligence research (activities may include training, fine-tuning, or improving large-language models; developing other kinds of artificial intelligence models or systems; and building virtual agents)" among the uses of Location Data, Driving Data, Vehicle Health Data, Voice Recordings, Exterior Image Data, Account Information and other vehicle data. The October version adds: "We collect and use personal information for the purpose of training large language models." The list of vehicle data covered by that section didn't change. Neither notice describes a separate way to opt out of AI or language-model use.
Change 3: Acxiom tracking across devices. The general notice already named Google Analytics and LiveRamp cookies. It now adds: "We also use cookies, tags, and similar tracking technologies, including those provided by Acxiom, to recognize visitors across different devices and browsers and to match browsing activity to broader audience profiles." It links Acxiom's opt-out page.
Change 4: AI in customer support and service messages. Customer support now includes "our use of third-party artificial intelligence models and/or other generative artificial intelligence technologies for customer support." In the Connected Services notice, the section on vehicle health reports, maintenance alerts and service-related marketing adds: "We may use third-party artificial intelligence models and/or other generative artificial intelligence technologies for these communications."
Other changes: Woven by Toyota and Toyota Research Institute are added to the affiliates Toyota receives information from and discloses it to. "Battery charge data" and "electricity consumed for charging" are added as examples of product data. In the Connected Services notice, the data sent to regulators now includes "battery energy data," going to "state and federal regulatory authorities," where July said "state regulators." The section on profiling and automated decision-making drops the line that, because Toyota doesn't make such decisions, "there is no need to provide a right to opt out." Connecticut residents are added to those who can ask for a list of specific third parties that received their data, and a Rhode Island list of third parties to whom Toyota "sell[s], or may sell" personal information is linked. The California "Shine the Light" section now points to the opt-out form at privacy.toyota.com.
What stays the same: the Connected Services notice still says Toyota won't share Connected Services Data with "Data resellers," "Social networks," "Ad networks" or "Insurance Providers, unless we have your consent or as required by law." You can still opt out of Connected Services or ask Toyota to deactivate data transmission.
How it compares (checked Oct 31, 2026): since July 1, 2026, Connecticut's privacy law has required a company's privacy notice to include "a statement disclosing whether the controller collects, uses or sells personal data for the purpose of training large language models" (Public Act 25-113, section 9). The statement is required either way, which is why the same phrase is now turning up in carmakers' notices, and why Toyota's October notice also adds Connecticut to the states whose residents can ask for a list of specific third parties. Toyota's answer is yes. Other carmakers' current US notices answer differently. Hyundai Motor America's privacy notice, last updated October 23, 2026: "We do not collect, use, or sell Personal Data for the purpose of training large language models." American Honda's privacy notice, effective June 3, 2026: "We may use artificial intelligence to perform some of these activities; however, we do not use personal information to train large language models." We found no statement about language-model training in GM's U.S. Consumer Privacy Statement (last updated June 17, 2026) or Subaru of America's privacy notice (effective July 1, 2026). Toyota's sister brand Lexus gives the same yes as Toyota.
Lexus: the Lexus Privacy Notice, updated October 14, 2026, has the same line, "For the purpose of training large language models." We didn't have an earlier Lexus copy to compare against.
Coverage (checked Oct 31, 2026): web, news and X searches found no reporting on either Toyota update. Open Terms Archive logged the change to the general notice on October 29.

entry.title: Canva e-signature terms (Oct 30, 2026): no ID check on signers, not an archive, no wills or POAs
entry.summary:
Canva published a new version of its Terms of Use, effective October 30, 2026 (the previous version was effective August 19, 2026). Section 6 was renamed from "Use of AI Products" to "Use of Products" and now opens: "Your use of certain Canva products and features may be subject to additional obligations and restrictions in the Feature Specific Terms." The footer of both the Terms of Use and the Privacy Policy now links a new document, "Canva's Electronic Signature Feature Terms."
Change 1: Feature-Specific Terms now sit inside the main terms. Canva's Feature-Specific Terms page (last updated 30 October 2026) says those terms "form part of" the agreement, and "in the event of a conflict" they "shall prevail" for the feature they cover. It lists terms for Affinity, Cavalry, Canva Sites and domains, the e-signature feature, beta features, printing and Brand Scan.
Change 2: New e-signature terms. Canva's Electronic Signature Feature Terms (last updated 30 October 2026) apply "whether or not you have a Canva account." Key lines: the feature "is designed for simple electronic signatures and is not an advanced or qualified trust service"; you "must not use" it for documents such as "wills, trusts, codicils, powers of attorney, and deeds"; "Canva does not verify the identity, age, capacity, or authority of any sender or signer"; and the feature "is a document workflow tool and is not an archive or evidence preservation service." Signed copies arrive as an emailed download link, and Canva "cannot guarantee" you'll receive or keep access to it. "Names, emails, and signing records will be visible to anyone who has access to the document or signing link," and signing records "do not constitute conclusive legal proof of signer identity, intent, or authority." Senders and signers, not Canva, are responsible for any E-SIGN Act consumer disclosures.
Change 3: Signers without an account are bound by Canva's main terms, including arbitration. The e-signature terms say: "If you don't have a Canva account: Canva's Terms of Use also apply to your use of the Electronic Signature Feature and use of Canva." Those Terms of Use (section 16(d), Dispute Resolution) send any claim "by binding arbitration by the American Arbitration Association (“AAA”) under the Consumer Arbitration Rules," require claims in "the parties’ individual capacity," and say "you and Canva are each waiving the right to a trial by jury or to participate in a class action." We found no arbitration opt-out in the October 30 Terms of Use (the only opt-out is for marketing messages). So someone who just opens a Canva signing link sent by a landlord, client or employer is, by Canva's terms, agreeing to them.
How it compares (checked October 30, 2026): Docusign describes "the standard way of identifying a signer" as sending "a link to the signer’s email address," which is roughly what Canva offers, and sells enhanced checks on top through Docusign Identify: government-ID upload with a biometric liveness check, knowledge-based questions, CLEAR, and one-time passcodes by SMS or phone. Canva's terms name no such option and leave it to senders to choose "signing tools appropriate to the sensitivity, risk and value of their transaction."
What stays the same: the rest of the AI section, including the separate AI Product Terms, is unchanged.

entry.title: SSA Client Data System (60-0392): new Social Security profile on every SSN holder, comments due Nov 30, 2026
entry.summary: The Social Security Administration (SSA) is creating a new Privacy Act system of records called the Client Data System (60-0392). The notice is on public inspection now and is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on October 30, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-22173, docket SSA-2025-0030). SSA says it will "track and manage information about a customer including personal information and customer interactions" and give employees "one main location to view information concerning the customer." The notice lists no history (it is a new system) and claims no Privacy Act exemptions. The published Federal Register document (91 FR 68581, October 30, 2026) says the new routine uses are effective November 30, 2026, and: "please submit any comments by November 30, 2026." Change 1: one profile for everyone with an SSN. The notice says the system "maintains information on individuals who have been issued a Social Security number (SSN), including those who have conducted business with SSA beyond enumeration." Records are retrieved "by the number holder's SSN." That covers anyone who has ever been issued a number, not only people who receive benefits. For comparison, SSA's existing customer-service records system (Appointments, Visitor Information, and Customer Service Record System, 60-0350, republished August 20, 2025) covers "individuals who visit an SSA office" or make an appointment. Change 2: what goes into it. The new system pulls data "primarily from existing SSA systems of records," and the notice names 12 of them, including the Master Files of SSN Holders (60-0058), the Earnings Recording system (60-0059), Claims Folders (60-0089), the Master Beneficiary Record (60-0090), the SSI record (60-0103), the Medicare Database File (60-0321), the Digital Identity File System (60-0373) and the Customer Engagement Tools system (60-0383). It also takes data from "third parties such as a contractor or vendor; and Federal, State, and local agencies." The record categories in one place include: name, SSN, sex, date of birth, parent names and place of birth; "country of citizenship"; mailing and email address, phone, language and texting opt-ins; "customer interaction history, including notes or remarks entered by technicians"; representative payee and appointed representative details, including fee agreements; benefit and SSI payment amounts; "yearly earnings and quarters of coverage"; accommodation needs such as Braille, interpreters or hearing loops; marriage details including the spouse's SSN, "reason for marriage end" and "marriage type"; "electronic block, high-risk, and special indicator warnings"; and indicators for the Defense Department's Wounded Warrior program and a VA "100% Permanent and Total Disability Compensation Rating." Change 3: a new use for your email address. The notice adds: "We may also use contact information (e.g., email addresses) provided by individuals who conduct business with SSA for program outreach (e.g., notification about our programs, online services, SSA events, and surveys) and other purposes related to our administration of the Social Security Act." We did not find that outreach wording in the source notices we checked (60-0350, 60-0383 and 60-0058). Other listed purposes include tracking "consent to text," identity verification, "prevention of fraud," research, staffing decisions and "agency strategic goals and funding decisions." Change 4: who it can be shared with. The notice lists 30 routine uses, which the published document says are effective November 30, 2026. Most match uses already in SSA's other notices. They include the Department of Homeland Security "upon request, to identify and locate aliens in the United States" under 8 U.S.C. 1360(b) (SSA's Master Files notice, 60-0058, already has this use); "Federal, State, and local law enforcement agencies and private security contractors" for office safety and related investigations; law enforcement investigating criminal violations of the Social Security Act; "private collection under contract with us" to recover overpayments; Treasury's Do Not Pay system; state agencies running Medicaid, TANF and food stamps (SNAP); contractors, other agencies and researchers under written agreements; and employers and private pension plans in situations where a person's whereabouts are unknown. SSA says it will not disclose IRS "return or return information" unless authorized. Is this the first shared SSA client database? No. A 2007 SSA privacy impact assessment describes an "Integrated Client Database (ICDB) System" that already shared "Client Data" (names, SSNs, dates of birth, sex, language preference, "their country of citizenship and the basis of U.S. citizenship") among SSA's claims systems, including for people not getting benefits. At the time SSA wrote that ICDB "does not require a new Privacy Act system of records" because the data was covered by existing notices such as 60-0058, 60-0090 and 60-0103. The new notice is different in three ways: it gives the combined profile its own system of records, its record list goes well beyond the identity fields the 2007 assessment names (interaction notes, marriage details, earnings, payment amounts and alert flags), and it states the email outreach and survey purpose. What stays the same: SSA says the data comes mainly from systems it already keeps, so the notice doesn't describe new information being collected from you. What changes is that it all sits in one SSN-indexed profile, along with interaction notes and alert flags that until now were kept in separate systems. You can't opt out of a system of records. You can ask for your record or contest it, but the notice says you "may need to identify each system of records in which the individual seeks to correct or amend the record" and follow each one's procedure. Coverage (checked October 29): we found nothing in news searches or on X about the Client Data System notice, which goes on public inspection on October 29. SSA's sharing of data with DHS under its Master Files notice was widely reported in 2025. This notice is separate. What you can do: comment by November 30, 2026 at regulations.gov under docket SSA-2025-0030, or by mail to the Head of Privacy and Disclosure Policy, Law and Policy, SSA, Room G-401 West High Rise, 6401 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21235-6401. Questions go to LP.PDP.SORN@ssa.gov or (410) 965-1727. If you'd rather not get outreach email or texts, check the contact and messaging preferences in your my Social Security account. To see what SSA holds on you, send a written request with your name and SSN to the system manager, with a notarized statement or a signed certification of identity.

entry.title: Grindr terms update Oct 27, 2026: AI summaries from chats shown to others, no refund if you turn AI off
entry.summary:
Grindr, the dating and social app for gay, bi, trans and queer people, rewrote its Terms of Service. The new version is headed "Effective Date: The earlier of October 27, 2026 or user acceptance." A help-center notice posted October 27 says: "If you don't agree with the updated Terms, you should stop using Grindr and close your account before they take effect." Grindr calls most of the edits clarifications meant to make the terms "shorter, clearer, and easier to understand." We compared the new terms with the previous version, archived by the Wayback Machine on October 6, 2026. Several of the changes are new rules, not just rewording.
Change 1: AI summaries about you, built from your chats, shown to others. The old terms already said AI may "assess and summarize past interactions to support reconnection and identify compatibility, and surface behavioral or engagement-based insights to You or other users." The new section 7.5(b) names chats and drops any link to whether you use the features: "Whether or not you use AI Technology features yourself, our systems may generate inferences, summaries, and other System-Generated Content about you (where permitted) from (i) your profile; (ii) your activity on the Services; and, (iii) , your interactions with other users including chats. We may share such content with users who use those features." The overview repeats that this content "may be shown to other users even if you do not use those features yourself," and 7.5(c) warns it "may be inaccurate, incomplete, or inappropriate."
Change 2: turning off AI can switch off paid features, with no refund. Under 7.5(d) you can manage how your data is used for AI "in your privacy settings in the Services, or via a request to our Customer Service team," but "If you turn a setting off, the features that depend on it may stop working for you." A new section 9.13 spells out what that means for subscribers: "Your Subscription and its billing are not affected by your settings choices. Turning off a setting is your choice and is not a change we make to the Services under Section 11; no refund is due except where the law requires it." The old terms had no such section.
Change 3: different prices for different users. The old terms said pricing "varies based on a number of factors including, but not limited to, region, bundle, and duration of subscription" and "We also test new features and payment options." Section 9.1 now says "we regularly test features, prices, offers, and payment options, so the Paid Features and prices you see may differ from those shown to other users."
Change 4: unsent and disappearing content. A new section 7.6 says expiring and unsend features "cannot retract content that another user has already seen, saved, captured (including by screen shot or screen recording), forwarded, or received in a notification," and "We may keep copies of expired or unsent content for safety, security, legal, and operational purposes as described in the Privacy Policy."
Change 5: mass-arbitration batching starts at 10 claims instead of 25. Batching used to apply when "twenty-five (25) or more individual requests for arbitration of a substantially similar nature" were filed with the help of the same law firms. Section 17.9 now applies when "10 or more individual Requests of a substantially similar nature" are filed, grouping them "in batches of 100" with one arbitrator per batch. That lets Grindr handle a smaller wave of coordinated claims together. A new section 17.10 says "No amendment will apply to a Dispute that accrued before the amendment's effective date." Under 17.13, existing users "may opt out of a material amendment to that agreement by sending an Opt-Out Notice that is received within thirty-one (31) days after we notify you of the amendment." Opting out "does not terminate or alter any prior arbitration agreement."
Other changes: section 4 now says "a new location-based feature may use your existing distance-sharing choice until you change it," and that someone may "be able to estimate your exact location or identify you" despite offsetting and blurring, which "may reduce this risk. They do not eliminate it."
What stays the same: Grindr already had a perpetual license to your content that included training AI ("to directly or indirectly create, develop, train, test, deploy, operate, and otherwise improve AI Technologies"). The new terms keep it, now "to the extent permitted by your privacy settings and the Privacy Policy." The 31-day arbitration opt-out for new users and the AAA mass-arbitration rules were also already there. Grindr's Privacy Policy is still dated July 6, 2026.
Coverage (checked Oct 28): we found no news coverage of the new terms. The only sources were Grindr's own help article and terms page, and we found no posts about the change on X.

entry.title: Slack: Slack drops "24/7 support" from its plan table; the free support tier now targets a 2-business-day reply
entry.summary:
Slack rewrote the support section of its pricing page. The plan comparison used to have a "Support" row headed "Access to customer support" with the entries "24/7 support", "24/7 support with 4-hr. first response time" and "24/7 priority with 4-hr. first response time". entry.title: Xero terms update Oct 2026: ID and biometric face scan verification, new US arbitration terms (Dec 28)
entry.summary:
Xero, the cloud accounting software used by small businesses, freelancers and their bookkeepers, posted new Terms of Use, new US arbitration terms and a new privacy notice, all dated October 26, 2026. The terms say: "The updates include the introduction of customer identity verification, updates to our dispute resolution process for customers in the United States, updates to section 31 and to the price change notification and cancellation processes for subscribers who subscribe to Xero via a third party platform. The updates are effective immediately for new customers, and from 28 December 2026 for current customers." We compared them with the previous Terms of Use (dated 3 August 2026) and the previous privacy notice (11 February 2025), both from Xero's own archive pages.
Change 1: identity checks, including a biometric face scan. A new section 12 says that to fight fraud and meet sanctions and anti-money-laundering rules, "we may ask you to provide things like government-issued identification documents and a biometric facial scan so we can confirm the document belongs to you." Third-party verification partners run the checks. "Your right to use these services depends on completing these checks to our reasonable satisfaction." If Xero can't verify you, or you don't respond in "a reasonable time," it "may decline to activate your subscription or restrict or terminate access to some or all of our services." The August terms had no identity-verification section at all.
Change 2: ongoing automated screening that can suspend you. A new section, "Keeping our checks up to date," says Xero may ask for updated ID "if your business structure changes or there's a change in ownership," and that "We also use automated systems to assess the risk of fraud, sanctions exposure or other regulatory non-compliance on your account on an ongoing basis." If those systems flag a risk, Xero "may suspend your access or limit certain features (such as payment features) while we look into it," and can terminate access if you don't satisfy the checks. For a business that keeps its invoicing, bills and payroll in Xero, a suspension means losing access to its own books until the check clears.
Change 3: the privacy notice now covers face templates. The new notice adds a "Verification and identification data" category: "We also may collect facial imagery and biometric data (including facial recognition templates) to match you to your identity documents and ensure it really is you when accessing our services through your login." That last phrase means face matching isn't limited to sign-up; it can also be used at login. Verification partners "may act as independent data controllers for certain activities" and "may also use anonymised or aggregated data across their network to improve fraud detection models." The February 2025 notice mentioned neither biometrics nor identity verification.
Change 4: US disputes get their own arbitration contract. The old terms had one sentence for every country: "you and we agree to resolve those disputes through binding arbitration or small claims court instead of in courts of general jurisdiction." US customers now get ten numbered rules. Before any legal action you must send a Notice of Claim to legalnotices@xero.com, and "you and Xero agree to meet via video or phone within 60 days to try and work it out. Both sides commit to showing up to that meeting personally." After that, small claims court "in your county of residence or in Denver, Colorado," or individual AAA arbitration. "You'll need to bring any claim within one year of when you knew, or reasonably should have known, of the issue." Arbitration is confidential: "Everything about the arbitration (including the proceedings, the evidence, and the final decision) stays confidential." If 25 or more similar claims come from coordinated lawyers, they are batched in groups of up to 50 and a few test cases go first while the rest wait. Xero reimburses your filing fee if you win, but if the arbitrator finds your claim frivolous, "you will be responsible for reimbursing Xero for fees and arbitrator costs we had to pay to defend the case." We found no opt-out.
Change 5: bank-feed aggregators disclaim liability for your bank login. Section 31 (bank feeds) now names aggregators "like Yodlee or Flinks" and adds: "If you use these services, you provide log-in credentials to your accounts at your own risk." Where local law allows, your bank and "our connected aggregators (and any third parties that interact with your log-in credentials or account data in connection with that bank feed) disclaim all liability for any loss, theft, compromise, or misuse whatsoever in connection with their service (including negligence)". The data "is not an official record of your account." The old section only said Yodlee feeds were "subject to separate Yodlee terms."
Other changes: "If the tax rate changes, we will adjust the tax amount charged on your next billing period without prior notice." Subscribers who pay through an app store or reseller may hear about price changes "through the standard processes used by the third party platform" and must cancel under that platform's policies.
What stays the same: you can still cancel a direct subscription "at any time by providing Xero with one month's notice," and class actions were already excluded.
Coverage (checked Oct 27): we found no news coverage of the identity-verification or arbitration changes. An automated change tracker, Rewindex, logged the terms page change on Oct 26; nothing on X.

entry.title: California sales tax on software and SaaS subscriptions starts Jan 1, 2027 (SB 122): what's taxed and what's not
entry.summary:
California is extending its sales tax to software, and the start date is fixed in law. Senate Bill 122 (Stats. 2026, ch. 23), approved June 29, 2026, rewrites what counts as "tangible personal property," the thing California's sales and use tax applies to. The state tax agency, CDTFA, puts it this way in its new tax guide: "Beginning January 1, 2027, sales and use tax generally applies to the retail sale of a digital product." A digital product is "prewritten computer software transferred on tangible storage media, transferred electronically, or accessed remotely," and CDTFA lists software as a service (SaaS) as one of them. California's statewide sales tax rate is 7.25%, and most areas add district taxes of 0.10% to 2.00% on top, so $100 a year of taxable software would cost at least $7.25 more.
Change 1: downloaded and cloud software stops being tax-free. Until now, California only taxed software sold on a disk or other physical media. The current rule (CDTFA Regulation 1502) says: "The sale or lease of a prewritten program is not a taxable transaction if the program is transferred by remote telecommunications from the seller's place of business, to or through the purchaser's computer and the purchaser does not obtain possession of any tangible personal property, such as storage media, in the transaction." From January 1, 2027, the amended Revenue and Taxation Code section 6016 says "tangible personal property" means either physical property or "A digital product and any copyright or patent interests associated therewith." The state's Legislative Analyst's Office summed up the old rule in May: the sales tax "does not apply to other sales of software, such as custom software, prewritten downloaded software, or prewritten software accessed remotely." That covers ordinary subscriptions to off-the-shelf software, whether you download it or use it in a browser or app. The law and CDTFA's guide don't name specific products. CDTFA's draft rules do address AI: an AI tool inside a prewritten platform is still not custom software, because its outputs come from "a generalized machine-learning system that is sold or licensed to many customers."
Change 2: what isn't taxed. SB 122 carves out most digital media. CDTFA says digital products do not include digital audio works (music, ringtones, spoken word and audiobooks), digital audiovisual works ("such as movies and videos with sound"), digital books ("such as electronic books"), digital video games played for entertainment, including in-game purchases, digital visual works such as computer-generated art, crypto and other digital assets, and cloud infrastructure and platforms that let a customer run its own software (IaaS and PaaS). Custom software written for a single customer stays exempt. So streaming video, music and audiobook subscriptions, e-books and games are outside the new tax, while productivity, creative, security and other prewritten software is in.
Change 3: subscriptions are taxed period by period, under draft rules. CDTFA released draft emergency regulations on September 1, 2026, held an interested parties meeting on September 10 and took written comments until September 24. They are not final. Draft Regulation 1600 says a subscription "is a continuing sale and purchase. Tax does not apply to payments received for subscription periods prior to January 1, 2027. Tax applies to payments received for subscription periods on or after January 1, 2027." Its examples: a one-time license paid on December 15, 2026 that can't be used until January 1, 2027 is taxable; software you get access to on December 15, 2026 but pay for on January 1, 2027 is not; and for a monthly subscription with a 12-month commitment starting December 15, 2026, tax "applies to the amounts charged for the continued right to access the digital product on and after January 1, 2027." Snell & Wilmer reads the draft as taxing an annual plan billed in November 2026 for the months after January 1, so paying ahead in December does not clearly avoid it.
Change 4: where you live decides, and you can owe the tax yourself. For software delivered online, SB 122 sources a sale to the buyer's known California address, starting with the billing address, then the shipping address, the mailing address tied to the payment method, and the mailing address. CDTFA says out-of-state sellers may need to register to collect the tax, and so may marketplace facilitators (app stores and similar platforms) that sell other developers' software. If a seller doesn't collect it, the buyer "may be responsible for reporting and paying use tax directly," including when software "is purchased for use in California from an out-of-state seller who is not registered with us to collect use tax or who is registered with us but did not collect use tax." Software bought outside California and used in the state within 90 days is presumed bought for use in California.
How other states do it: California isn't the first state to tax cloud software, but it leaves out more than some. New York's tax department says "prewritten computer software is taxable whether sold: on a disk or other physical medium; by electronic transmission; or by remote access." Texas taxes SaaS as a data processing service: the Texas Comptroller says "Data processing services providers include sellers of software as a service and application service providers," and "Twenty percent of the charge for data processing services is exempt from tax." Washington goes further than California. Its Department of Revenue says "Sales or use tax apply to all digital products, regardless of how they are accessed (downloaded, streamed, subscription service, networking, etc.)," a list that starts with "Downloaded digital goods (music and movies, etc.)," and it taxes remotely accessed software too. So California's version taxes software like New York and Washington do, but unlike Washington it leaves streaming, music, audiobooks, e-books and games out.
How much money is at stake: when the Governor proposed the tax, the administration estimated it would raise $450 million for the state General Fund and $560 million in local sales tax in 2026-27 (half a year), and $900 million and $1.1 billion a year after that, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, which called those estimates reasonable. The LAO also noted that a large share of the newly taxed sales will likely be businesses buying software, and that such taxes are often passed on to consumers anyway.
Coverage (checked October 26): accounting and law firms (PwC, Deloitte, EY, RSM, BDO, Snell & Wilmer and the National Law Review) have written it up for businesses, and on X it came up in a political trend on October 18 about the number of tax increases Governor Newsom signed. We found no consumer news story explaining which subscriptions it covers and which it doesn't.
What you can do: check your bills in January for a new tax line on software subscriptions such as office, photo and video editing, antivirus, password managers and AI tools. Make sure your billing address is right, since that decides whether and at what rate you're taxed. Don't expect prepaying an annual plan in December to dodge it: under the draft rule, tax applies to subscription periods from January 1, 2027. If you buy from a seller that doesn't charge California tax, you may owe use tax yourself. Before you cancel anything, note that streaming video, music, audiobooks, e-books and entertainment games aren't covered.

entry.title: AT&T arbitration and terms change Nov 1, 2026: 60-day wait before small claims, JAMS replaces AAA
entry.summary:
AT&T is replacing the dispute-resolution rules in its Consumer Service Agreement, the single contract that covers AT&T wireless (postpaid and prepaid), AT&T Internet and Fiber, Internet Air and AT&T Phone. AT&T's summary page says: "the updated AT&T Consumer Service Agreement will apply to you starting on November 1, 2026," and "By using or paying for AT&T services on or after November 1, 2026, you are agreeing to the terms." Anyone who got or changed an AT&T product on or after September 1, 2026 and agreed to the new terms is already on them. Customers say AT&T emailed the notice in mid-September. AT&T keeps the old text at att.com/priorcsa, titled "AT&T Consumer Service Agreement (Prior to September 1, 2026)". We compared it with the new agreement line by line.
Change 1: small claims court now comes with a 60-day wait. The old agreement's plain-English summary said: "you can choose to file your individual claim in small claims court or send us a Notice of Dispute, which is required before starting arbitration." The Notice and its 60-day "Informal Resolution Period" only gated arbitration: "Any arbitration proceeding cannot be commenced until after the Informal Resolution Period has ended." The new text reads: "Any arbitration or small claims court proceeding cannot begin until after the Informal Resolution Period has ended." So before filing in small claims over a bill dispute, you now have to send AT&T a signed Notice of Dispute and give it 60 days (longer if either side asks for a settlement call). If you skip it, "a court of competent jurisdiction can enjoin the filing or prosecution of an arbitration or small claims court proceeding."
Change 2: AT&T gets more time to make the offer that decides whether it owes you $10,000. If you win in arbitration and the award beats AT&T's last written settlement offer, AT&T pays at least $10,000 plus double your lawyer's fees. That offer used to count only if made "before the arbitrator was selected." Now it counts if made "before the arbitration record closes," and the comparison is "not counting attorneys' fees, costs, and expenses." AT&T can wait until late in the case, after it has seen your evidence, to make the offer that sets the bar.
Change 3: a new arbitration provider and a new place for hearings. JAMS replaces the American Arbitration Association, under the "JAMS Streamlined Arbitration Rules and Procedures." Hearings used to be "in the county (or parish) of your billing address"; now they "will take place in a location reasonably convenient to you." An arbitration demand must now include "a certification of compliance with the Informal Dispute Resolution Process" signed by you and your lawyer, and "must disclose any person or entity that is funding or has a financial stake in any aspect of the arbitration."
Change 4: mass claims can end up in court, still one person at a time. When 25 or more customers with the same or coordinated lawyers bring similar claims, each side now picks 20 test cases instead of 25, followed by mediation, twice. After the second mediation, either you or AT&T can "opt out of arbitration and elect to have your dispute heard in a court." You must send a signed notice "within 30 days after the second mediation ends." A new Section 1.12 makes the class-action and jury-trial waivers apply in court too: "each party may bring claims (whether in court or in arbitration) against the other only in an individual capacity." The old line pointing Puerto Rico customers' small-claims cases to the Telecommunications Regulatory Board is gone from the arbitration section.
What stays the same: AT&T still pays JAMS fees on claims of $75,000 or less that you start (as long as "there is no dispute that you have fully complied" with the notice step), you can still bring issues to the FCC or other agencies, and the Notice of Dispute can still be submitted online (att.com/noticeofdispute). (Cricket, which AT&T owns, is making the same changes on December 1 but has dropped its online Notice option.)
Can you reject it? Subsection 1.3.2.8 lets you reject a change to the arbitration provision "by sending us written notice via U.S. Mail within 30 days of the first notice of the change" to Legal Department – Revised Arbitration Opt-Out, AT&T, 208 S. Akard, Office #2900.13, Dallas, Texas 75202, with your name, address, phone number, account number and "a statement personally signed by you." Rejecting keeps the prior version, which lets you go straight to small claims. If your first notice was the mid-September email, that window has likely closed. Rejecting does not get you out of arbitration altogether. The only other choice AT&T offers existing customers is to cancel all AT&T services before November 1.
Coverage (checked October 25): a few customers posted the AT&T email on X in mid-September (the largest got about 100 views) and r/ConsumerArbitration noted the switch to JAMS. We found no news coverage of the small-claims wait or the settlement-offer change.
What you can do: if you have a billing dispute with AT&T that you planned to take to small claims, submit a Notice of Dispute now, online at att.com/noticeofdispute or by mail to Legal Department - Notice of Dispute, AT&T, 208 S. Akard, Office #2900.13, Dallas, Texas 75202, so the 60 days start running. Keep a copy and the date AT&T received it. If you got AT&T's notice in the last 30 days, mail the rejection letter above and keep proof of mailing.

entry.title: FCC robocall and text opt-out rule (Nov 25, 2026): companies can make reply STOP the only way out
entry.summary: The Federal Communications Commission has rewritten how you can stop automated calls and texts, and the change has a start date. The final rule (FCC 26-67, "Enhancing the Ability of Consumers To Control the Robocalls") went on public inspection on October 23 and is published in the Federal Register on October 26, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-21821), with this line: "Effective November 25, 2026." The FCC adopted it on September 30 and released it October 1. It covers the robocalls and robotexts that need your consent: autodialed or prerecorded calls and automated texts to your phone, such as payment reminders, delivery and appointment alerts, bank notices and marketing texts. Change 1: the company can choose the only way to opt out. Today's rule, in effect since April 2025, says you can revoke consent "by using any reasonable method to clearly express a desire not to receive further calls or text messages," that a reply in other words must count "if a reasonable person would understand those words to have conveyed a request to revoke consent," that a voicemail or email to the company creates a presumption you opted out, and that callers "may not designate an exclusive means to request revocation of consent." From November 25, the rule says "Callers may designate any of the following methods as the exclusive means to revoke consent": an automated voice or key-press opt-out on the call; replying to a text with one of seven words ("stop," "quit," "end," "revoke," "opt out," "cancel," or "unsubscribe"); or a website or phone number the company picks. A company that does this "is not required to process revocation requests made by any other means." In practice, if a sender has named reply-STOP as its method, a text like "please take me off your list" or "no more messages," an email to customer service, or telling a phone agent may no longer legally count. The company has to disclose its chosen method "clearly and conspicuously" on the call or in each text, and texts only need to mention one of the seven words, but the sender must still honor all seven. Companies that don't pick an exclusive method must keep accepting any reasonable request. Change 2: stopping one kind of alert no longer stops the rest. The rule now says callers "may interpret a revocation request made in response to an informational call or text message ... as applying only to the specific category of informational robocalls and text messages to which the revocation was directed and not to all communications." Replying STOP to a payment reminder can leave the same company's appointment, delivery or account texts running, and you may have to opt out of each type separately. The FCC's example is a consumer who stops payment reminders but still wants fraud alerts. This replaces the 2024 "revoke all" rule, which would have made one opt-out cover everything from that sender. That rule never took effect: it was put on hold by waiver, most recently until January 31, 2027, according to Nixon Peabody. Marketing is different: a STOP to a telemarketing or advertising message still revokes consent to all future marketing robocalls and texts from that caller. Change 3: banks get more numbers to call without asking. Under the FCC's exemption for fraud and security alerts, banks could send these to a cell number only if "provided by the customer." From November 25 they can also use a wireless number "obtained from a reliable source," meaning one "supplied by a spouse or other family member who is authorized to be on the account; obtained when the customer calls the financial institution; or included in records obtained from another financial institution." Opt-outs and the exemption's limits on how many calls and texts can be sent still apply. What stays the same: companies must still honor an opt-out "within a reasonable time not to exceed ten business days," a one-line confirmation text is still allowed, and senders that use texting systems that can't receive replies must say so in each text and offer another way to opt out. More could change. In a companion proposal (FR Doc. 2026-21820, also published October 26), the FCC asks whether to cut the ten-business-day deadline (it floats seven), require two-way texting, require a one-step "revoke all" option, and how opt-outs should apply to a company's affiliates. Comments are due November 25, 2026, and replies December 28, 2026, in CG Docket No. 02-278. Coverage (checked October 24): law firms and industry groups (Nixon Peabody, DLA Piper, Manatt, Crowell & Moring, Orrick, the ABA Banking Journal and the Ecommerce Innovation Alliance) wrote it up for businesses in late September and October. We found no consumer news story explaining what it means for people who want the calls and texts to stop, and on X only a handful of small posts. What you can do: from November 25, read the opt-out line at the bottom of an automated text and use exactly that word (STOP is the safest), or the number or link it names. On robocalls, use the key-press option if one is offered. If you want all of a company's automated messages to stop, reply to each type you get (reminders, alerts, promos), or ask the company to stop everything through its named method and keep a screenshot. Opt-outs must be honored within ten business days, so keep a record of the date. To weigh in on the follow-up proposal (for example, asking the FCC to require a one-step "revoke all" option or a shorter deadline), file a comment by November 25 in CG Docket No. 02-278 through the FCC's ECFS system.

entry.title: Fitbit API shutdown Oct 30, 2026: reconnect MyFitnessPal, wellness and other apps in Google Health or they stop syncing
entry.summary: Google is switching off the old Fitbit Web API, the connection that lets other apps read data from your Fitbit account, on October 30, 2026. Google's developer site says: "On October 30, 2026, the Fitbit Web API will be turned off and will no longer function or sync data to or from Fitbit users." The original cutoff was the end of September. On September 28 Google posted a "one-time 30-day extension" to developers, and it says that on October 30 "the legacy Fitbit Web API infrastructure will be decommissioned and permanently turned off." Apps have to move to the new Google Health API, and the switch can't happen silently. Google's migration guide says "existing access and refresh tokens cannot be transferred, requiring users to re-consent to your updated integration." In other words, every app you once linked to Fitbit needs you to sign in and approve it again. What it means: if you use a Fitbit with a calorie counter, a training app, an employer or insurance wellness program, or a research study, that app stops receiving new steps, sleep, heart rate and workouts after October 30 unless you reconnect it. The Google Health app (the Fitbit app's new name since May) now warns: "To keep syncing your fitness, sleep, or wellness data without interruption, reconnect your account through the partner app before October 30, 2026." Google also says it can't fix a missed connection for you: "Google Health Support can't restore or fix your broken connection once Fitbit connections retired on October 30, 2026. Reconnection must be enabled by the partner app's developer." If an app shows no reconnect option, Google says "the app developer hasn't released their updated integration yet." Apps that sync through Health Connect on Android or Apple Health on iPhone are not affected; Google says "your data will continue to sync as usual." Data already in your Google Health account is not deleted, according to Google. What the apps are telling users: MyFitnessPal (help article updated October 19) says members "will need to reconnect the integration in order for data to continue syncing," and warns that "If you already reconnected MyFitnessPal and Google Health after receiving communication from Google, you will still need to complete this reconnection again when prompted by MyFitnessPal." The same page lists a known issue, status "Investigating": "Some members are reporting exercise and Step data is not syncing from Google Health after disconnecting and reconnecting." Personify Health, an employer wellness platform, tells members: "The deadline for reconnecting is October 30. After that, syncing through the Fitbit connection stops." The University of Minnesota's HR office warned employees on October 8 that anyone who uses a tracker to "earn wellness points" needs to reconnect "by October 30 to continue syncing your activity data." Strava has changed too. Google's help page says "Activities logged in Strava will no longer sync to Google Health via the Strava integration," and if you don't update the Strava connection, "only bikes, runs, hikes, and walks with GPS will continue to sync" from Google Health to Strava. For research participants, Fitabase, a platform many Fitbit studies use, says the reconnect option stays in the Google Health app "Through November 30, 2026" for people who miss the deadline. Google also extended demo accounts used in studies through December 31. Coverage (checked October 22): tech sites covered the Fitbit app becoming Google Health and Google forcing the last holdouts onto the new app (Android Authority, The Verge and TechRadar, around October 12). We found no news story about the October 30 cutoff for connected apps. It appears on Google's developer pages and help center, app help pages, and one small review site's X post. What you can do: open the Google Health app, tap Connections at the top left, then Partner Apps, and look under "Needs Action." Tap "Tap to reconnect" where it appears. For apps marked "Reconnect in partner app," open that app, go to its connected apps or integrations settings, choose Google Health or Fitbit, sign in with the Google Account you use for Google Health, and grant the permissions it asks for. If your wellness program pays rewards for steps, check after reconnecting that new days are showing up. A gap could cost you points.

entry.title: Shein terms change Oct 21, 2026: customer support is now "a courtesy," not an obligation, for carrier, bank and seller problems
entry.summary: Shein updated its U.S. Terms of Use today. The top of the page now reads "Effective Date: October 21st, 2026" (the previous version was dated September 3, 2026). Open Terms Archive recorded the new version on October 21, and the only substantive edit is a new Section 17, "Customer Support": "SHEIN may, in its discretion, assist with questions about the shipment, delivery, return, refund, or payment of an order, and will handle customer service inquiries in a reasonable manner. Unless a SHEIN policy expressly states otherwise, any such assistance is a courtesy and does not create a contractual obligation for SHEIN to resolve issues caused by carriers, banks, payment processors, Third-Party Sellers, or other third parties. Where a third party's involvement is necessary to resolve your issue, we may refer you to that third party." The old Section 17, "International Users," becomes Section 18. Nothing else in the U.S. terms changed. What it means: when a problem traces back to someone other than Shein, such as a delivery company losing or delaying a package, a bank or payment processor declining or double-charging a payment, or one of the marketplace sellers whose items Shein lists, the terms now say Shein's help is voluntary and that it can send you to that company instead. This matters because Shein is also a marketplace. Its terms already say the Services "enable users in the United States to purchase products from third-party sellers" and that "SHEIN neither owns nor takes title to any product sold by a Third-Party Seller" and "is not an auctioneer, seller, or carrier of any items that are listed for sale by Third-Party Sellers." The new wording has a limit: "Unless a SHEIN policy expressly states otherwise." Shein's existing written promises still apply. For example, the same terms still say claims for "loss or damage during delivery of the order by the carrier" must be made to Customer Service "within fourteen (14) days" of when you received the goods or should have received them, and that if Shein finds the claim valid it will replace the item or reimburse the purchase price and shipping. Returns still follow Shein's Return Policy. So the change mainly covers everything those policies don't spell out, and it gives Shein written backing for telling you to contact the carrier, your bank or the seller. Like all changes to Shein's terms, it applies as soon as it's posted: Section 1.2 says "By continuing to use or access any of the Services ... after the posting of changes, you accept and agree to any such changes." The arbitration agreement and its 30-day opt-out (written notice to us_legal@sheingroup.com within 30 days "after first becoming subject to this Arbitration Agreement") are unchanged. Coverage (checked October 21): we found no news reports or social posts about the new section. What you can do: for a lost or damaged package, file with Shein Customer Service within 14 days, since that promise is written into the terms. Save order pages, chat transcripts and tracking screenshots. If Shein or a seller won't fix a charge for something you never got or that wasn't delivered as agreed, you can dispute it with your card issuer. For credit cards, the FTC says the Fair Credit Billing Act dispute letter must reach the issuer "within 60 days after the first bill with the error was sent to you."

entry.title: IPL (ipl.org) is shutting down Nov 9, 2026: download your uploads first (accounts and data deleted)
entry.summary: IPL, the essay and study-help site at ipl.org, is closing. A help-center article titled "Important Update: IPL is Retiring. Everything You Need to Know." (dated September 28, 2026) says: "Effective November 9, 2026, IPL will be officially retired" and "After that date, the site will be taken offline permanently." Nothing moves elsewhere: "We are not migrating any content or product features from IPL to a new platform." The article says the shutdown lets the company "channel our energy into other Learneo businesses" and points students to Course Hero, QuillBot, Scribbr and LitCharts. Accounts: "After this date, logins will be disabled and you will no longer have access to your user account." If you can't log in, IPL says to email support@ipl.org "before November 9, 2026. We may not be able to help after support winds down." Your uploads: "You can download everything you've uploaded to IPL before it closes on November 9, 2026. We'd recommend doing this sooner than later." After that, "you won't be able to access your account or retrieve your content." Public pages: "Public pages on IPL will stop being available after November 9, 2026," though "search engines and third-party archive sites may keep cached copies for a while, which is outside our control." Data: "we will delete user accounts and data," but "we may retain certain user information for a limited period of time following November 9, 2026." IPL also says it isn't "selling, transferring, or licensing user-uploaded content to anyone, and we won't use it to train models or build other products." Billing: "All recurring charges will be stopped before November 9, 2026." Subscribers with time left past that date "may be eligible for a prorated refund," and IPL says support "will reach out to you directly." Some history: the ipl.org domain once belonged to the Internet Public Library, a nonprofit online library that opened on March 17, 1995, was later run by a consortium headed by Drexel University, and stopped operating in 2015. The site that reopened on the domain around 2020 is a commercial essay repository, which is the service now closing. Coverage (checked October 21): apart from IPL's own help page, we found no news reports or social posts about the shutdown. What to do: log in and download anything you uploaded, especially essays you wrote yourself and don't have elsewhere; if you link to your public IPL pages from a portfolio or class site, save copies now; if you're a paying subscriber, watch the email tied to your account for the refund notice, and contact support@ipl.org before November 9 if you can't get in.
